utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the witness now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let him take the oath, please. Witness P (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the appearances of counsel now? You can take your seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Teresa McHenry, trial attorney for the Office of the Prosecutor. I'm here with my co-counsel, Mr. Giuliano Turone, and our case manager, Ms. Elles van Dusschoten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Now appearances for the defence, please. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. My name is Edina Residovic, defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. With me is Professor Eugene O'Sullivan, Professor from Canada. MR. OLUJIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Zeljko Olujic, defence counsel of Mr. Zdravko Mucic. With me in the defence team is my learned colleague Mr. Michael Greaves, attorney from the United Kingdom. MR. KARABDIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. My name is Salih Karabdic. I am defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic. With me in the team is Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am John Ackerman, representing Esad Landzo. With me is Cynthia McMurrey. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. McHenry?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Sir, am I correct that you have requested that your name not be made public as part of your testimony here today and that your face not be shown publicly? Can you hear me, sir? You don't have to do anything. You can just answer and I believe the ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (In interpretation): yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You will be referred to as Mr. P here today; is that all right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, showing you what has been marked on a piece a paper, a name, can you just confirm that this is your name and then I'll give it to the Registrar so that the record is clear? Is that your name, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'll just ask that it be given to the Registrar. I don't know if defence counsel wants to see it, but they have already been advised of the name. Sir, how old are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm 42. I will be 43 shortly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: How are you employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, how are you employed? What kind of work do you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm working as a doctor specialist of otohinolaryngology in a medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is otohinolaryngology -- is that also an ear, nose and throat specialist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Could you just briefly summarise your education?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed elementary and secondary school in Konjic, the School of Medicine in Sarajevo. I attended three semesters of post-graduate studies at the Department of Surgery with anaesthesia and re-animation. Due to the war I was unable to continue my education, my specialisation. I also completed specialisation in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Where were you living in the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was living in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you left Konjic, Konjic town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only during my specialisation and during the war operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: During the war operations can you just tell us when it was that you left Konjic town and where you went, just briefly, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact dates, but I think I left Konjic in the second half of April, somewhere perhaps around 25th. Up till then somewhere between 10th and 17th April 1992 the director of the medical centre, Dr. Ahmed Jusufbegovic called us Serbs doctors and there was a lawyer amongst us who was also Serb, a lady, and he warned us to seek shelter for our families, because allegedly he was being threatened by Serbs. I proposed that I would be prepared to act as his personal guard. I didn't take this seriously. However, upon the arrival of the HOS forces in the motel in Konjic I realised that the situation was serious and I should try and seek shelter for my family. I do not remember the exact date when I left. It could have been 20th, 21st or 22nd, I'm not sure. I headed in the direction of the village of Bradina. In the meantime, before I left and before I decided to leave for Bradina, in the office in the medical centre Miroslav Stenek arrived. He was my former maths teacher. For the last ten or fifteen days -- years, I'm sorry, years, he was working in the SUP, in the police. What kind of job he did I don't know. He advised me to seek shelter. He proposed I go to Lake Boritz or Bijela. I asked: "How am I going to get through when there are checkpoints on the outskirts of Konjic?" He said the least I should do was to go to Bradina. I consider this to have been his friendly advice.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We have to object at this time. This is non-responsive to the question and I would like to ask that the witness just answer the question asked by the Prosecutor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Carry on with your statement. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to fetch my family by car and in Pozaraz I came across barricades. I couldn't pass. I had to go back. Then the telephone rang in my apartment. I answered and they told me that I was free to cross the barricades. There would be no more difficulties. I was allowed to pass through the barricades. I reached Bradina. I learned later that in Bradina at the checkpoint a group of Muslims who were going from Konjic in the direction of the Podbitolje villages -- Repovci, Stojkovici, Bulatovici -- had been stopped at the barricades. I spent the day there and I think maybe it was the next day, most probably the next day, I went back to Konjic again to work. This went on for several days. I don't know exactly for how many. I think somewhere up to 5th or 6th May, because there was a bus going from Repovci via Bradina to Konjic, and it was transporting workers, and I used that bus. In the meantime it happened on several occasions that I could not reach my work post and I called Dr. Jusufbegovic to inform him that I was unable to reach the centre. On one occasion he gave me approval. When he was going to Repovci he visited me at my home. He talked to me and my father and said: "If you don't manage to come in a couple of days, there will be no problems." That was the oral advice that he gave me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, can I just ask you: during the time that you were in Bradina, living in Bradina, was there any organised armed defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regarding the military organisation and defence, all I know is that the people organised themselves. It was self-organisation. I had no weapon. I was working in an out-patient clinic, and I was arrested in my white coat, together with the wounded in my surgery. Two had gela (sic) wounds. One had --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am going to have to object right now. The question was: "In Bradina was there any organised defence?" I am asking the court to please ask the witness to answer the question the prosecution is asking him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please kindly interfere less. Let her lead the witness the way she wishes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you: you have indicated that you yourself were not armed. Were you any part of the organisation of the defence of Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If one can describe it as participation, I was working in the out-patient clinic. Therefore, if I had any duty and if anybody wanted to ask me such a question as a provocation, my answer would be that I worked as a doctor in my surgery.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. So is it a fair summary that, although some people had organised themselves and some people were armed, am I correct that you were not armed and you were not part of that organisation, the defence organisation I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, were you part of any political organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I did not belong to any political organisation, nor did I participate in the Republic elections in November 1991. This was my personal sign of protest, because I did not agree with the political parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, were you part of any negotiations going on between persons from Bradina and persons from Konjic about the various defence concerns that the various communities had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I don't at this point -- I'm not going to ask you any specifics about that. I just wanted to clarify that you were part of that. Let me go forward, sir. Was there any military action in Bradina in May of 1992 that resulted in your capture or arrest, and, if so, can you please tell us when this was and what happened to you specifically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Before the major offensive there was some exchange of fire along the confrontation lines. I don't know exactly where those lines were, because I wasn't there, so I cannot say, but on 25th May 1992 somewhere around 1 o'clock in the afternoon the shelling of Bradina started.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Where exactly were you, sir, when the shelling started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the surgery. Next to me was my colleague, Edhem Seper, and for a time Risto Zuza was there too. We were sitting on logs in front of the surgery under an apple free.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: At some point were you captured or arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On 26th May 1992 I was arrested in my surgery, wearing my white doctor's coat. There were some locals with their hands behind their heads heading towards the dispensary, and behind them were soldiers wearing camouflage uniforms. I saw that they had the insignia of the HVO and the TO. I was searched in front of the clinic and then taken to a collection point in front of the cafe in Bradina. A column had already been formed and just behind the school on the road, the local road, heading towards Ivan Sedlo on the road near the school, women and children had been gathered together. Then they -- after making us line up in twos to form a column, we went on foot forwards Konjic. We covered about 1 or 1.5 km., because the tunnel had already been blown up, that is the tunnel leading from Bradina towards Konjic on the main highway. As we went, they beat us with rifle butts, they kicked us and they forced us to sing Ustasha songs. It was horrible to see them beating old people and forcing them to sing Ustasha songs. I remember one of them: "The star shines above Metkovic and bring back our Ante Pavelic". That was the song. Then near the tunnel they loaded us onto trucks. As far as I can recall, I was in a truck of brand name Tam, T-A-M, 2001. I don't know whether it belonged to the electrical distribution firm of Konjic or the company Sipad of Konjic. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, where were you taken after you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After our arrest we were taken in vehicles to the sports hall in Konjic. As we came out of the vehicle there was a double line of soldiers wearing camouflage uniforms, and as I came down, somebody hit me hard on the head. I lost my glasses. I tried to pick them you. Somebody trod on them and then the beatings started. They beat us with metal rods filled with sand, which we saw later on. They were the kind they used in the camp later on. Then they used rifle butts. They kicked us. Rifle magazines were used. Then we were led into the corridor of the sports hall. I know that I had to go on my knees to the dressing room. We had to bend our heads. If anyone were to look sideways, he would be beaten additionally, though the beatings went on all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, how long did you spend in the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We weren't there for long. We were kept in the dressing room. These are my estimates. I'm not sure, but I know they were kept there 20, 30, 40 minutes on the outside. Then they picked us up again and they told us that they were going to take us towards Grude, that it was by mistake that we had been brought there. Then they loaded us onto trucks. I was in a van which had the words "Oslobodjenje" on it which means it belonged to the Oslobodjenje publishing house. They brought us to Celebici. There were two or three men there. I think that they were not wearing camouflage uniforms. They beat us during the ride there. With me in the van was Slavko Zelenovic, Milan Zivak, his son Dragan, Milan Zuza. How many more of us were there I can't recall at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, would this have then been on 26th May that you arrived in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You've indicated that your glasses were broken. Just can I ask, going ahead a little bit, at some point were you able to get replacement glasses, or did you never have your glasses again while you were in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got glasses when I was transferred from the health centre in Konjic, and I can tell you how this happened, in the elementary school called Third May.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I just wanted to establish that you got some later. Can you please tell us what happened when you arrived at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we got off the small van or bus there was again -- there were two lines of soldiers again. They beat us and they forced us to climb a truck, on to the body of the truck. As I didn't have any belt my trousers slipped a little, so I found it difficult to climb. They kept beating me all the time. Next to me was Jasmin Guska, Chief of Department of SUP, and Sevko Niksic, chief of the Konjic police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me just clarify. When you say next to you were Mr. Guska and Mr. Niksic, do you mean that they were also being detained, or do you mean that they were there but not part of the people being detained or beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not detained. They were officials belongings to the authorities at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Just please continue with what happened to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, as I was saying, I passed through this double line, and whatever they asked, I had to answer, and with every new question the beatings intensified. I managed somehow to climb onto the truck. There was a boy in a camouflage uniform on top. He pushed me down again so I had to climb up again and be beaten again. When we managed to climb onto the truck, it moved maybe a couple of metres only and they told us that they were taking us to Grude. Then again they ordered us to come down. We did and we had to line up against a small wall in front of the entrance to Number 9. It must have been some kind of a nuclear shelter of the former military barracks in Celebici. We had to raise our hands up. They took my -- personally they took my wallet, my bank card, a signed cheque, money, and they didn't see my watch so they didn't take my watch. They were beating us all the time. I asked Mr. Guska: "Should I take off my white coat?" "No", he said, "you have to be like that". Then I had to take my shoes off. I entered Number 9, but I begged Milan Zuza to hold my hand, because I couldn't see very well. It was very dark as you entered. I somehow felt my way and entered Number 9. The other prisoners entered as well. I believe they went through the same procedure as myself, and about half an hour later Rale Musinovic came. I can't remember just now what his proper name was. He was a driver in the transportation company of Konjic. He introduced himself as the camp commander. He said that a number of military policemen had violated orders and that they would be punished. We begged him to bring us water. A guard brought some water. We drink. In the meantime he called me out and told me to go with him to work in the health centre in Konjic. Coming out of Tunnel Number 9 Marko Ruzic was waiting for me. I think he was a soldier in a camouflage uniform -- no, there was another soldier in camouflage uniform, Ulas. I'm afraid I don't know his name. I don't even know his parents, because I knew the parents of many others, the families, wives and mothers. So we sat in a car and they took me to the house of Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, can I stop you for one moment? Let me go back for a minute. When you stated for you your wallet and money was taken as well as identification, were any of these items ever returned to you, the money or the identification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The driver's licence was not returned. The signed cheque was not returned. The bank card was not returned. Later when I was practically released into house arrest I asked Zeljko Buric, the driver, if he could find those documents for me. He only brought me back my personal ID and he asked me whether I had been wounded. I told him: "No". Then he said, "Where is the blood from? Were you beaten? Where were you injured?" "In my head." Then on my personal ID he said: "This is probably your own blood on this card."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, was your money ever returned to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never and I wouldn't even want it back.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that you were brought into Tunnel 9. How long did you stay in Tunnel 9 before you were taken out and brought somewhere else; in other words, was it an hour, was it over the night? Can you just tell us how long you spent in Tunnel 9 before you were taken out again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About one hour. I was brought to the house of Mr. Delalic and I waited there for a few minutes. They went in to announce me. I went up to Mr. Delalic. Mr. Delalic was sitting. I think that he was wearing his morning coat. Across from him was Dinko Zebic. I think he was a commander of the HVO. We exchanged greetings. He asked me --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me stop you for a minute. Can I just go back? So when you say Mr. Delalic was wearing his morning coat, was this in the morning that you met Mr. Delalic or in the afternoon of 26th? MR. OLUJIC (in interpretation): (Not translated).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The interpretation is not coming through.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the question -- the objection? MR. OLUJIC (in interpretation): Yes, your Honours. We have an objection. The witness did not mention the hour and the date about when this happened, and so it is suggestive and leading, the question that the Prosecutor is asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you on the same objection too? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): No. The objection is putting the -- the witness said that Mr. Zejnil Delalic was wearing a morning coat and not a suit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The question was: at what time did you go there? A morning coat, does it suggest he went there in the morning or the afternoon? I don't think counsel talked about any suit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I think there may have been an interpretation issue. Sir, maybe this could clarify: am I correct that you went to Celebici on May 26th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 26th May.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And if you remember, sir, can you tell us the day and the approximate time, if you know, that you were brought to Mr. Delalic's apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was brought at night. That was the night of 26th, 27th, and I think it was about 4.00 am. I found Mr. Delalic at his house and he asked me whether I was hungry. I told him I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, can I just go back for one minute just so I can clarify? So am I correct if it was 4.00 am, it would have been the early morning hours of 27th May, just so I can clarify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can I also -- when you say you met with Mr. Delalic at his apartment, can you tell us, if you know, the first name of Mr. Delalic and where this apartment was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The apartment was across the street from the gas station in Konjic. Mr. Delalic used to have an auto-mechanic shop and carwash shop and then that didn't work out. Then he opened a disco there. I was only once in his disco, not after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, when you say Mr. Delalic, do you know the first name of the Mr. Delalic that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do know. Zejnil.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Going back now, could you please tell us exactly -- I know you have been trying to -- could you please tell us exactly what happened when you went to Mr. Zejnil Delalic's apartment? Please continue with exactly what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic offered me a dinner. He offered me a drink. I refused that and he offered me coffee. I had coffee. He offered me a cigarette. We lit up. Then he said to Dinko Zenic: "Look what your Ustashas have done to him", because I was all covered in blood. Then he offered me to go and wash up in his bathroom. I went there and I told him -- I could see all the black and blue marks on my face at that time. I returned. He asked me if I knew where the machine-gun nests were and I told him only that I knew that there was a point at the entrance and I only knew that there was something at Mico's cafe. He said: "How did you know that because there was no electricity there?" Mico had a generator there, so I was trying to use that and at that time when I went, I could see the stacked sleepers. Then he called doctor Ahmed Jusufbegovic on the phone and I heard -- in fact, he spoke to someone from the emergency centre. I heard him say: "He has to come right away, even if necessary in his pyjamas. He won't sleep. Let him call me again." Ahmed Jusufbegovic, he called him again and told him: "Relja is here and he's coming your way."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me just make sure that it's clear. When you went to Mr. Delalic's house, did he initially call and speak directly to Dr. Ahmed Jusufbegovic or not; when he first called trying to get hold of the doctor who did he speak to or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He called the emergency service, and because after 3.00 pm the phone exchange is switched over to them and I don't know who he was talking to, but he was asking for Dr. Ahmed Jusufbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I see. Who is Dr. Ahmed Jusufbegovic? Did he have any relation with the health services in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was the director of the Health Centre and Mr. Delalic told him -- he saw my wounds and he said: "Treat this and he should work. If there's a soldier need to protect him, then let a soldier protect him." Then we said goodbye and his secretary gave me a box of cigarettes and some matches, because he demanded that she bring me this. Then I went to the Health Centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me go back a minute. During this conversation in addition to telling Dr. Ahmed Jusufbegovic that you were supposed to work, was there any other discussion, even if it wasn't about you, that you heard Mr. Delalic's side of? Did they discuss anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He asked them why people from Repovci did not take part in the attack on Bradina. I don't know what Dr. Jusufbegovic told him, but I heard again: "Check on that, and if they are not there tomorrow morning, they should return all the weapons to Bradina."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who was it who said if the people from Repovci weren't there the next morning --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. He doesn't know who said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm clarifying. I think there's just a clarification issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Delalic was speaking to someone on the other side.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am not asking him what the person on the other side said. I am trying to clarify what he heard Mr. Delalic say. I am not sure the record is clear. Sir, when you indicated -- who was it, if you know, who said: "Check on this or the people from Repovci and if they're not there tomorrow, they have to return the weapons"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic. Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You have answered the question. You have answered it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, after your conversation with Mr. Delalic, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken to the Health Centre in Konjic, to the emergency ward. He told me to take off my coat and really it was all bloodied and dirty, and I did that. I was -- I had it over my arm, and Dr. Vjekoslav Mandic met me there. There was a nurse there. Her name was Jadranka Kovacevic. They told me to lie down. Vjeko looked at my wounds and I told him: "No, there is nothing wrong here". I said: "I don't need to be sewn up or anything". They gave me my coat back. Dr. Ahmed Jusufbegovic came at that point. I won't forget this. Vjeko and Jadranka treated my wounds. They put Band-Aids and together with Ahmed Jusufbegovic I went to the Maternity Ward. There Ahmed Jusufbegovic asked me whether people from Repovci took part. I said I did not know. I was in the dispensary. He said that this was madness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How is it all relevant for us? You can expand your direct examination to any extent. Let's have something which is relevant for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I believe much of what has been said has been relevant, but let me go forward, sir. Sir, did you -- without getting into the details, how long did you spend working in Konjic hospital? Just tell me how long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent the night, so that is that morning and the next night, the following day, so that means two days, that morning, the next night, and then the following day I went to the Third March Elementary School.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you: at that time was the Third March School being used as a school or being used as something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no classes. They were interrupted. When I came to the Third March, I found there some wounded, who had been brought back from Celebici, which means that somebody had looked at them and gave them medical help in Celebici. I don't know when, at what time that happened. Subsequently I heard that Dr. Rusher and Dr. Vjeko had come and I think also Dr. Jusufbegovic, but I'm not sure about this. I only heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, was there a period of time that you worked at the Third March School treating the injured persons from Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Just tell me approximately how long was that? How long did you work at the Third March School?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think up to ten days. I don't know exactly but I think up to ten days.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: How did you know that these injured persons that you were treating -- how did you know that they were from Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They told me that themselves. Some had been arrested at the same time that I was. For instance, Srda Gligorevic was arrested at the same time when I was. Marko Mrkajic was also arrested at the same time as I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me go forward. In addition to telling you they were from Celebici, did any of these persons tell you how or where they obtained their injuries? You don't have to tell me the specifics of what people told you. Can you just tell me if any of the persons told you how they obtained their injuries or where they obtained their injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While being beaten, when they were being beaten, that's when they received those injuries. There were fractures of arms, of the pelvis, of --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me just go forward. Did any of these persons tell you whether or not they received these injuries while being beaten in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Celebici

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you just please estimate how many persons there were with significant or severe injuries from Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were about 20 of them, 25, and after that it climbed up to about 30 injured.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir -- I'm sorry. Can we have the translation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we had there -- I believe ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, was one of the persons you treated Mr. Slobodan Babic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Third March Elementary School no -- yes. Yes. Slobodan Babic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was Mr. Babic himself able to say anything about how he received his injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He was unconscious.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What happened to Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was told by the prisoners that he had been beaten up. However --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. Let me clarify. In terms of his medical condition what was the course of Mr. Babic's medical condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got there we didn't have any medicine, and after a couple of days Dr. Zrinko Brekalo came with Mihajlo Magazin, who was a technician. They came to look, to treat the injured, and Zrinko in the end said: "Do it yourself and write down what you need of medicine". I wrote down. I asked for analgesics, antibiotics, a lot of different medicine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, can I just direct you more specifically, can you please tell us exactly what you observed about Mr. Babic's injuries and what, if anything, happened to Mr. Babic as a result of the injuries you observed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were haemorrhages throughout the body. I put a Foley's catheter there and I saw that the urine had blood in it. I tried to put something on his mouth and some water, but everything kept coming back through his nose. I wanted to see what had happened inside and part of his palate had been injured, both the soft tissue and hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is he a cousin of Mirko Babic that appeared before us?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I don't know. There were so many people of the same name. Do you know if Mr. Mirko Babic and Mr. Slobodan Babic are related?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Because Mirko Babic has told us where Slobodan Babic received his injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe a number of witnesses have testified about Mr. Slobodan Babic, including that he was injured in several locations, including in Celebici. So that's why I'm asking this. I'm sorry. The witness doesn't know if there's any relation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I was just asking you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, please continue with what you observed about Mr. Babic and what happened to him. You were saying that the inside of his mouth was injured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Some of the prisoners told me that they were giving him -- that they had put the barrel of the rifle inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, at this point I'm just asking you to tell us what you yourself observed about his injuries and what happened to Mr. Babic as a result of his injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was unconscious. I managed to look inside his mouth and the soft tissue of his palate and part of the hard part, and I put a bag over Foley's catheter, and the urine came out bloody.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What happened to Mr. Babic as a result of his injuries, if anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He died within two days.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to say whether or not he died from his injuries that you observed and have described?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have an objection that I need to make for the record. That is that this witness is now being asked to testify as an expert and was not listed by the prosecution in accordance with the court's order as an expert, but simply as a fact witness. So I would at this point object to this witness giving any opinions as an expert witness regarding cause of death and things of that nature, since he has not been properly designated by the prosecution as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I may respond just briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we have had this discussion before. The Prosecution believes and certainly interpreted the court's order about expert witnesses to not include witnesses such as this witness, who was really a mixed fact -- potentially an expert witness. I still can't say that he has been called here as an expert witness. His statement which was part of the supporting material and given to the defence at the time that their clients made their first appearance contains in detail what this witness says, which includes the fact that he was a doctor and treated people. It's also the case that earlier in May after the prior -- when it became clear that there was potentially some disagreement between the defence and the prosecution concerning what was meant by the court's order about expert witness, we supplied the defence counsels with the curriculum vitae of this witness and another witness and specifically told them that these witnesses would be testifying consistent with their statement. So I don't believe that there can be any argument that the defence has been unfairly prejudiced and, in fact, we plead that -- and I can find case law that in cases where someone is a mixed fact/expert witness, without necessarily being called expert witnesses, they are permitted to testify about what they observed and their conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, back in April I believe I filed a written objection to Dr. N testifying as an expert witness, and I'm sure the Tribunal recalls it and is familiar with it. I just adopt those arguments as an objection here to save everybody some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it is clear for the record, the CV presented to the defence is less than one half-page and contains virtually no information. So to the extent that the court might have believed that we were supplied with something significant, we were not. The proposition that if an expert has also some factual knowledge and can be designated as a fact witness that they somehow lose their character as an expert witness is simply incorrect. An expert witness is someone who is called for the purpose of giving opinions to the court based upon their expertise. The difference is between relating what you observe and what your opinion is about what you have observed. To the extent that this witness is being asked to give medical opinions based upon his observation, he is clearly an expert witness, and we should clearly have been advised that he was being called as an expert witness and given all the material that went along with the court's order in that regard, and therefore giving us the opportunity to conduct the kind of background investigation and things of that nature that that would give us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Slobodan died in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: He died in the Third March School --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That was converted into a hospital?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: A makeshift hospital infirmary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That I think he can depose. He was very seriously injured and he died in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I believe that this witness can and should be permitted to give his observations about whether or not there is any relation between the injuries he saw and his death. I think in cases where someone is a mixed fact and expert witness, someone may be permitted to gave their opinion, and it's a matter for the court to determine the weight to give that. This has been in the supporting material and it includes this witness's observations, including why someone died. As soon as there was any question, we provided all the material to the defence, and this is the first we've heard that they are going to object to this. So I believe that this court should allow this witness to give his observations. You may give it what weight you deem appropriate and the defence may cross-examine about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us hear you. MR. OLUJIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honour. First of all, it is true that the witness should convey all he knows, all that he is familiar with, and there is no objection to that, but both in common law and continental law an expert witness is an assistant of the court. Therefore, he has to have certain references. I fully respect the witness and I do believe that he is a nose, ear and throat expert, but on the basis of half a page of a CV I cannot assess whether he is qualified to give opinions on injuries. So let the witness limit his remarks to the observations he made. If he saw certain injuries he may say so, but to make any opinions about them is impermissible, unless he acquires the status of an expert witness in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I'm not too sure what your objection is that you have. Is it the brevity or the quality of his qualification? Is it because the CV is too short or that he is, in fact, not a doctor or did not work in that place as a doctor?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, to the extent you are asking what my objection is, it is that he was -- that this court entered an order that the Prosecution had within a certain period of time to designate any expert witnesses as experts, that they were going to call, and supply significant information to the defence about each of those witnesses. That has not been done with regard to this witness, and for Ms McHenry to say she had no idea we were going to make this challenge is incomprehensible, because they did this before with Dr. O, who they said they didn't think was an expert witness, that he was just a fact witness, and we challenged that and the court essentially agreed that he should have been designated as an expert and was not permitted to give expert opinions, but only to testify as to his lay person kinds of observations and the things that people told him that had happened to them. So I'm not objecting to this witness saying: "Slobodan Babic had a cut on his arm", or, "Slobodan Babic was bleeding from his nose", or things that any of us could observe. My objection is to: "Give us your opinion as to his cause of death." That is something none of us can do. It requires expertise to do it. I am not sure there has been an establishment of the qualifications of this expert sufficient for this court to accept him as an expert on pathology specifically. There is no indication that he did any kind of an autopsy with regard to this particular individual. I am not just objecting to that particular question but any questions that ask for an opinion about any of these injuries. I don't have any problem with him describing the injuries that he observed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think you have got sufficient material. He treated him. He knows what his injuries were. The fact that he died within two days in the hospital, that should be sufficient. We can draw our own conclusion whether he died as a result of injuries or bad treatment or whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe you can, but I argue that even if he is not an expert pathologist, this witness can and should be allowed to give his opinion. There is much case law which says things such as: "If a witness possesses special skills and experience, even if he is not classified as an expert, is a matter for the Tribunal. It is reasonable that the ..." -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That a person is died is one of common knowledge. You don't have to take a doctor to tell us that a person has died. Anybody can say that. If he is dead, he knew of the event and he can say so as a person who was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I certainly agree with that and I don't understand the objection. I certainly agree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The objection is that you are putting forward an expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That's right, your Honour. With respect to that, I don't believe that his opinion has to be considered an expert opinion. I believe that to the extent that this objection is a technical objection about exactly how the defence was notified, I think it's not appropriate. There was and there continues to be disagreement about whether or not this witness is considered an expert witness, which is why he was not on the list. After the defence brought this up with respect to Dr. O, we immediately gave them their CVs, which they have had for well over a month. If they are dissatisfied with the quality of the CVs, they certainly could have brought that up before, or they can cross-examine the witness about it. So I just believe as a legal matter that this witness should be allowed to give his opinion about what he observed and his reasonable conclusions, drawing on his special skills. This court may give it the weight it deems relevant, and certainly he was not a pathologist. Certainly he did not have the ability to do autopsies. Certainly your Honours also may be able to, even without any evidence, make your own conclusions about likely causation, but the issue is: should this witness be permitted to give his observations for the court's consideration? The prosecution believes he should be able to and that there can be no prejudice to the defence. The argument is a technical argument, on which they cannot be prejudiced, and we, in fact, still disagree about the merits, but to the extent that there was any issue about his qualifications, they were given his CV a significant time ago, and if they were dissatisfied, they have could have asked us, or they can cross-examine about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the long and the short of my objection to Dr. O's testimony, which is the same as it is here, is that this Trial Chamber entered an order saying: "We'll do something if the prosecution does something, if the defence does something to designate these folks, and if you have to designate one late, go ahead and do it and we will look at it if there is good cause". Presumably the decisions of this Trial Chamber are more than ink on paper. They ought to mean something. It was the middle of April that I filed my objection to Dr. O. That's, what, ten weeks ago now. The prosecution has made no attempt to designate this man as an expert witness. Ten weeks is plenty of time to sit down, do a CV, write a motion to the Trial Chamber saying: "We want to designate this guy as an expert."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Which count relates to Slobodan Babic's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe it's counts 13 and 14, your Honour. Let me ... yes, your Honour, counts 13 and 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Cecez, Slobodan Babic ... okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The witness is not testifying as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness is testifying as a fact witness, which necessarily encompasses the fact that he had special skills and experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think that's a different matter. When he has such special skill and in respect of which he can pronounce opinions based on those skills, then you regard him as an expert, but in these circumstances that is not what he is doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. So in that case may I ask him the question? I'm not sure that I understand your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You are leading him to say exactly what happened to the person he was dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, and I have asked him for his conclusion about whether or not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is why the defence objects. It is not his conclusion. What actually happened is what counts, not whether that was his conclusion. What happened was that the person died. The conclusion is what he draws from what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That's right, your Honour. We believe that he should be allowed to give this, and in this case the defence has been on notice from the date of the initial appearance about the substance of this witness's testimony, and after the issue with Dr. O, although we stated that we continued to believe he was not being called as an expert witness within the meaning of this court's order, we immediately gave them the CV, so that there could be no argument about it. The situation with Dr. O, who was not a detainee in the camp, and whom the defence did not have the CV of in advance is an entirely different matter. So if your Honours were to disagree with the prosecution and find that he is an expert witness, we would be seeking permission to ask him -- to designate him both as an expert and fact witness and as grounds we would state because he is a mixed fact/expert witness. He wasn't in it. But the defence has not been prejudiced because they have had the statement for over a year and they have had the CV for six weeks, so that there can be no argument that the defence is not prepared for this. In that regard we specifically sent them a letter with the CVs and said: "We will seek to have him testify consistent with his statement."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you can ask him the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I wonder whether I might offer a contribution? It's a short one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: My learned friend Ms McHenry has described this gentleman as a man with special skills who is going to give his opinion about things. Surely the English language means that that is an expert. I put that proposition to your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He wasn't brought in for that purpose. If he was --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: If he was, the normal procedural background would have been laid for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The fact of the matter is that the prosecution admit he is an expert in the terminology of the English language. Someone with special skills who gives his opinion means he is an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually an expert doesn't necessarily jump into the expertise. There is a foundation for the expertise and that foundation is the facts on which the opinion is based. So this is the normal route. You just don't come in and pronounce that this is your conclusion. Those conclusions are based on certain facts. He is able to make a pronouncement because of his special skill.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Which others cannot. Now where perhaps one has some difficulties whether the rules have been complied with, probably they have been, definitely he could now go on and give his opinion as it should be. That is your main problem, whether you have actually complied with the rules. There is no point talking about the person being a mixed fact and expert. Either you are an expert or you are not. If you are an expert, definitely you must base your opinion on that, so it definitely follows, but for you to be able to show that you have complied with the provisions, then that should be sufficient to accept him as an expert witness for the purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do I understand then that I may ask the witness this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can, provided you can satisfy the objections that you made the proper -- complied with the proper conditions of the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In effect you have already got enough material. The man was very seriously injured and he died two days later. Now if you want to ask him about the cause of the death, then it opens a very wide field. Did you get a pathological test done? Did you see his heart condition? So many things come in. Why do you want to open that field? . He was very seriously injured. He dies two days later. That should be sufficient for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree it is sufficient and if this witness is not permitted to make this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You need the provision of expertise because he was there, he was dealing with him and he died.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I'm not permitted to ask this witness whether or not he observed or he concludes that there's any relation between the injuries and the death, certainly the prosecution believes that we have nonetheless -- the circumstances are such that the court can itself draw its own conclusions. So I agree with your Honour in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is what he said fifteen minutes earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right. I believe his conclusion, because he was there and did have special skills and experience, is relevant, even though it may not be -- certainly the prosecution sometimes asks questions which may not be in every case necessary but it believes are relevant and of assistance to the Chamber, and that's why I would ask that I be permitted to ask this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You can ask this question but you are not relying on his skill. This is what we are saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, what, if anything, are you able to say about Mr. Babic's death and any relationship it might have had with respect to the injuries that you observed and have testified to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You see, this may lead to another question. Did he have the pathological tests with him? Did he have -- he might have died from some other cause. He might be suffering some other disease also in addition to the injuries. That I said opens a very wide field. Why do you ask him this?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Because the prosecution, with all due respect, believes that it's relevant, around certainly the fact that there was no pathological examination, but, your Honour, I believe with respect to everyone who was killed in Celebici, the circumstances were not such that they were immediately brought and an autopsy was done and we have the report. So we have to rely on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Not only the pathological test; what his past medical history is also. He might have a heart or other problem also. You have opened up a very wide field.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe all those things go to weight. The circumstances were such that the people at Celebici, we may not have their entire medical histories --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Did he carry out a post mortem examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: We can ask that, your Honour, and I believe the answer will be no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So how will that help you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Because I believe these matters are relevant to weight rather than to admissibility, and the fact is in this case we are not going to and in this war situation and certainly in Celebici the fact that those in authority did not take appropriate measures such that we can just easily give your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually we have wasted too much time on a very simple issue. Here is a person who was looking after him. He died. He can say he died. He doesn't have to be an expert to say that. It's not necessary. Don't tie it to his special skill because you have not established that he has those special skills.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, in that case, your Honour, again if I understood you correctly, sir, without going into your skills as a pathologist or lack of skills as a pathologist, as a person who was there treating Mr. Babic, are you able to say anything about the relationship between the injuries you saw and cause of death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You are going back to the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Same question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is not the issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If your Honours tell me that I'm not allowed to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: What happened to the gentleman after his injury, just that; what happened?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, I have asked that, so I will move forward with this. If the prosecution believes it necessary, we may file a legal brief on this, but I will move forward for now, because I understand your Honours to have upheld the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Sir, just so your Honours know the next question is presumably -- well, can you just -- I was just going to say it was a long one in terms of your timing, but I will just move forward. Sir, can you please tell us how your stay at the Third March School ended? What happened such that you left the Third March School and where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can I ask that the witness's microphone be placed on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, will you continue, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we stayed there about ten days -- I do not know exactly how long -- in the Third March Elementary School. Then one evening Mr. Pavo Mucic arrived and he called me out into the corridor outside the classroom where we were working and he told me for security reasons we needed to be moved. He read out the names of some people who were taken away, and I later learned that they went to the Musala sports hall. Dr. Milan Zuza went with them. We were taken back to Celebici, to building Number 22.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Prior to the war did you know Mr. Pavo Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I knew Mr. Mucic before the war. His brother's wife went to elementary and secondary school with me and we were quite close while we were studying in Sarajevo. He came to visit me, to the surgery on several occasions. I granted him (sic) leave. We would get together occasionally downtown. So I did know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Before the time he came and talked to you and directed that certain people go to Musala and certain people go to Celebici, had you seen Mr. Pavo Mucic at the Third March School?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before that he did come. Mr. Mucic came on a number of occasions to the school. I know once he sat with me in the corridor. He asked me what had happened to my face and head. I said: "Well, you see the bruises". I showed him my back. He said: "Your back is broad enough so they resisted the beatings. Your back resisted the beatings".

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: During any of these prior occasions did Mr. Mucic say anything to you about his role with respect to the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that he was being forced actually to take over command of the Celebici camp, and that he should become commander shortly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Approximately how many days was it before Mr. Mucic told you that he was taking over the command and the time when Mr. Mucic came, separated those persons going to the Sports Hall and Celebici? MR. OLUJIC (in interpretation): Your Honour, objection. The witness did not say to take over command of the Celebici camp. That was said by my learned colleague, the Prosecutor. At least that's how the interpretation came out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose if that's the interpretation ... What the witness said and I heard was that Mucic said he was being forced to take over. He was being forced to take over. That is why the question: "How long from the time he said this to the time he actually took over?" That is why that question, and I think it's quite appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you are permitted to answer the question. Will you please tell us how long the period was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps a couple of days before we were moved from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Can he recall the month when he came and told him he was being forced?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I'll ask him, but given that he was in -- sir, am I correct that from the calculations that you were moved from the Third March School to Celebici approximately ten to twelve days after you were first arrested or ten to fourteen days after you were first arrested on 26th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The last version I think is correct. I spent about two days in the Health Centre, then about some days -- ten days in the Third March School, and then we were moved to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. So it would have been somewhere around 10th June that you were moved to Celebici approximately, and it was a couple of days before that that Mr. Mucic told you that he would be taking over the -- taking over as commander of Celebici camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that he was being pushed into taking over command of the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we'll have a break here and come back at 12 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Sir, you have indicated that some time around June 10th you were brought to Celebici. Now I'll ask you more questions later about the details of when you were released from Celebici, but just for now to give the judges an overview such that they can understand your answers, can you just tell us how long you stayed as a prisoner in Celebici, meaning that you were detained there 24 hours a day? Just tell us when it was that you stopped being a prisoner there, meaning you stopped being kept there 24 hours a day. Just the date, please, if you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 22nd July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: After that time, 22nd July, when you were released, did you continue to go to Celebici during the day to treat injured detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Again, just for the overview, when was it then that you stopped going to Celebici during the day? When was that that you stopped having any contact with Celebici at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe about six or seven days before my escape.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When was your escape? When you say "escape", do you mean escape from Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Konjic. I can talk about that later, if I am permitted but after my release on 22nd July 1992 I remained in Konjic for three or maybe around three days and then I went to Ostrozac and then I escaped from Ostrozac.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When was it that you have left Ostrozac and the entire Konjic area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Ostrozac from the Konjic area, that is the Jablanica Municipality, that was 16th October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So am I correct that around 6th October you would have ceased having any contact with Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think around 10th October.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You're right. I'm not a mathematician either. Sir, going back to when you were brought to Celebici some time in early to mid-June and kept as a prisoner, can you just describe where you stayed in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was put in the Building Number 22, which was a storage room for water pumps and that was in the former barracks of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you first came to Building 22, was it being used to store water pumps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. The building -- when we were brought in there in this Iveco van -- I think that the Auto-transportation Company of Konjic was the owner -- the beds had already been brought in there and they were made up, so that we would move the injured people straight to those beds that were already there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you were at Celebici, was Building 22 then used as a kind of infirmary or makeshift infirmary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what it was called, yes. It was called the infirmary. However it was just Building Number 22.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Could you describe it, including its functioning as an infirmary? In other words, can you explain what kind of facilities were there, the equipment, medicine? Can you give us an idea of how this infirmary exactly worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Concrete floor underneath, then there were two small windows there, maybe 30 by 20 cm. The roof was made of tin. The door was metal. They opened outwards. Around the walls -- the beds were placed against the walls and in the middle just a plain -- that is an office desk. There we had a drum with gauze. We had one pincers. We had one scissors, and I think that was all as far as the equipment was concerned, and some medicine. A good part of the medicine that we received -- I said that Dr. Zrinko Brekalo came and Mihajlo Magazin, who was the technician, they visited us, and after that they brought the medicine with them and they said it was a donation by Caritas. This really helped us a lot. We brought that to Celebici and we used that quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: During the time that you were in Celebici, was there any procedure for requesting additional medicine? Were you ever able to request additional medicine from people in the camp and, if so, how did that work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was told to write down the request for the medicine, and we did that, and we would give it to Mr. Delic for the most part, and he would go and then whatever he would bring back. I don't know what the procedure was for him, how he went and acquired those medicines. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you requested medicine, were you able to always get what you had requested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, we did not. A very small portion of the medicine is what we would normally get. For the most part these were analgesics. There were some antibiotics. We also requested -- because there were elderly people there we asked for diuretics and those are generally what we were requesting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you have any diagnostic equipment? Were you able to perform surgery? Were you able to send persons to the hospital? Can you give us an idea of how those things worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We could not send people. In fact, once I requested when I was in the Third March School -- Doko Kuljanin needed to go to the oculist but he was not taken there. When I got back from the Health Centre Marko Mrkajic, Srdo Gligorevic came with me. In other words they were already given some medical help in the Health Centre because Gligorevic had a fracture and he was placed -- a splinter was placed on his forearm.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: While you were in Celebici were you ever able to send anyone to a real hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us something about the kind of files that were kept? Were there medical files for the prisoners? Did you have any prior medical history records? What kind of records were you able to keep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The medical -- we did not have the previous medical records on the detainees' health conditions, but we requested to be given a protocol. So that would be just a notebook where we would enter the data, the last name and the therapy we were giving and the nature of the injuries. I don't know if it was Mr. Delic or Mr. Mucic who brought this, but they did bring this to us and we were also given a pencil so we were able to write with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you in a position to be complete and accurate in this notebook in the records you kept and, if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could keep an accurate record of the name and last name and date of birth, but as far as the diagnosis was concerned, I was afraid that somebody may check on what I was writing down. So I was really writing down a very light diagnosis. In other words, I did not dare write "a fracture of the forearm". I would just say it was a blow to the forearm. That's how I did it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to this notebook?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what happened to it. However, I know that later when I would come from my house arrest I saw that parts of this notebook were used as cigarette paper, because the detainees had already started -- this was several days before I did -- before I was released that they were given food, and then they had also some tobacco but did not have any cigarette paper. So they used this as cigarette paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Am I correct that you don't have this notebook now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't be allowed to take it with me either. That is a medical record that could have cost me my life.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Besides you, sir, was there any other doctor who worked in the infirmary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There was another one. There was another doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You don't have to give their name now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, were you ever interrogated while you were a prisoner in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I gave a statement. I think his name was Pajic. He was an active sergeant in the JNA before the war, and I gave the statement to him. It was approximately -- it was approximately half a page long. That was the A4 size.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Approximately when was it that you were interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Maybe four or five, maybe even seven days but I'm not exactly sure. I don't know exactly the date when I was interrogated but I did give a statement and I did sign it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Is this maybe between four and seven days after you were brought to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you ever told anything about why you were being imprisoned or if you were placed in any particular category?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion talking to Mr. Mucic I found out that there were about ten categories there, and I asked him to tell me what category I was in, and he said: "According to some criteria you belong to number one and according to some, to none."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, as part of your work in the makeshift infirmary, did you have occasion to treat any injured prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It came out that way, that I did treat, which is normal, because I would give them medicine, I would listen to them -- on them with my stethoscope. I could measure their blood pressure. I could see if this was bronchitis, if it was an asthma attack, if it was inflammation and whatever medicine I had, I could give them so it would relieve -- bring them some relief, but it wouldn't be a real full type of treatment, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did any of the -- did any persons die while they were in the infirmary, and, if so, would you please just tell us their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were Pero Mrkajic. I think he was born in 1927, 1928, maybe up to 1930. Bosko Samoukovic. They died in the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Besides those two who died actually in the infirmary, was there any other person in the camp that you examined their corpse or had occasion to see the corpse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had an opportunity to see a corpse of Cedo Avramovic. He was a teacher. He arrived in the morning. In fact, Broceta arrived in the morning to see me -- I can't remember his first name -- and Hebibovic -- I think his first name is Ismet, the first name. I'm not sure. Duko Dutic -- it was a Duko Jelo. I went to Hangar Number 6 with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Where was it that you saw the body of Mr. Avramovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to object to the relevancy of questions on this individual. I'm asking what the relevancy of these questions about Mr. Avramovic has to do with the indictment. It's not in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, in general we would -- I would first state for the record that the indictment charges superior responsibility for murders, including some named individuals, but that evidence of other murders would be relevant to this charge. In fact, for this I would also state that certainly any evidence about how corpses were treated, what kind of investigations there were after people died, is relevant to the general conditions at the camp, and it's for that reason that I'm asking it. I don't plan on getting into much detail about these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you satisfied?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: With all due respect, your Honour, the indictment lists specific names. This name is not among them. It's not in the indictment. It's not relevant in this case, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is not completely irrelevant if it shows a pattern of behaviour. Yes, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The corpse was in Hangar Number 6 in the far part of it. Somewhere in the middle, midway on the right side of it, there was a metal pillar there and I looked at the corpse. I saw a laceration and contusion on the head and the chest. There was a bruise on the chest. I don't know more about that. Then I was told to carry out the corpse and then we did that. Broceta demanded that we did it, that we perform religious ritual on it. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know what happened ultimately to the body of Mr. Avramovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know. I know that Broceta told me that he attended the funeral, but where and when the body was taken I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Going back to Mr. Mrkajic, can you please tell us what you yourself observed about Mr. Mrkajic and his condition, what you observed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I looked at Pero Mrkajic. I examined him, and he had haematomas on his back and on his legs, the upper part and the lower part, and I think on the one hand he had -- I checked for inflammation. There was no inflammation. I know that Pero Mrkajic had -- this was before the war -- he had a latent -- that means diabetes. That would be typical for the elderly people, which he controlled by diet. I know that when Mr. Pavo Mucic came, he asked me what was going on with him, and I told him that he was a diabetic, and then he pulled out from his pocket insulin and he had an extended effect, and he said that I knew the laboratory results and also there was no smell of acetone (sic). It is not acetosis and it could be treated with insulin.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Haematomas, are they contusions or bruises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I am not sure if I fully understood. Did you treat Mr. Mrkajic for his latent diabetic condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pero died the next day after he had been brought to the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you give any more description or tell us how extensive the haematomas that you saw were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fairly large haematomas on the back and on both upper legs and lower legs. I couldn't tell you the exact size.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry. Did you -- I'm not sure I understand. Did you give Mr. Mrkajic any insulin? If not, why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not give the insulin to him, because he had not used it before, and you start using it after the laboratory analysis, and it is easy to cause diabetic complications. However, I did not have an opportunity to check on the laboratory results, and I could not smell the acetone. So he had not suffered any. The diabetes did not enter into its complications. So it is a visual method to work out laboratory analysis.
