utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Tell me if I have understood you correctly, sir. You did not treat him for his diabetes because you did not smell acetone, which would have indicated that he was in severe need of insulin, and you were afraid to give him anything absent that, because you didn't have laboratory results. Is that a fair summary of what you have stated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is. Then there is imbalance of minerals occurring at that time and I would not like to belabour this. I don't want to now give a lecture in medicine to the Trial Chamber. I just did it in a very brief way, that I explained this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you explain to Mr. Mucic that you should not give insulin without laboratory exams?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and he told me to do as I thought was best.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately when this was that Mr. Mrkajic died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In July.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: With respect to Mr. Avramovic, if you can, can you give us an approximate time period when Mr. Avramovic died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was about the end of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Going back to Mr. Mrkajic for a minute -- I'm sorry. Now going to Mr. Bosko Samoukovic, please, can you tell us with respect to him what you observed, how he came into the infirmary, who brought him and what you were able to observe about his condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a sunny day. It must have been after midday, and I first heard some blows and screams. I think that this beating went on for a long time, 20 or 30 minutes, but shortly he was brought in. He was being carried by the inmates into the infirmary. They were followed by Mr. Esad Landzo, a guard, and when I asked, because it is common medical practice to ask about an amnesia, and when I asked they said that he was suffering from a disease and he was placed on the second bed to the right. We laid him down and I asked him: "Bosko, what happened?" He said that he had been beaten by Mr. Landzo. I measured his pulse. It was very low, very weak breathing. I started to examine his chest. It was very painful. Then I could feel that a rib had been fractured. Whatever I had as therapy I administered to him, and after 15 or 20 minutes he passed away, he died.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can you explain exactly was you mean when you asked about amnesia and they said he was suffering from a disease? Can you explain exactly in some more detail what happened there? I'm not sure I understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An amnesia means to enquire what -- means he had -- whether he had suffered any traumas, whether you had lost consciousness. Can he reconstruct the event fully, and suchlike questions. Usually the injured would be carried in and when we would ask them what was happening, the guards would say that they were epileptic, that they had fallen in an epileptic attack and had got injured, but as I knew Bosko from before the war, I knew that he was not suffering from epilepsy. He was a railway worker and they had regular annual check-ups. He was working at the rail junctions, so they would not have been assigned such a responsible post if they were epileptic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, did you have any conversation with Mr. Landzo when he accompanied the prisoners bringing Mr. Samoukovic in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He said to me: "If he's not ready by 6.00, you get ready."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What did you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It meant that I should get ready to be beaten, for a beating.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What did you understand that: "If he's not ready by 6.00", to mean, "he" meaning Mr. Samoukovic -- what did you understand by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I expected that they would come back to fetch him again to beat him again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: In addition to noticing that his chest was painful and that a rib had been broken can you just tell us what, if anything, you were able to observe about how Mr. Samoukovic appeared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His condition was poor. He could hardly breathe. He was fighting to catch his breath. I'm not competent to qualify the injury, because only a pathologist can -- is fully qualified to assess the injury, but on the basis of my clinical examination and palpations I made, I was able to establish that there was a fracture. I was unable to do any X-rays. That was not allowed, because I too was a detainee, and if I asked for anything, I would get beaten more, so that I had to protect myself too.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, in addition to your clinical examination, were you able to see anything about how he appeared, without going into technical examination? Were there any other signs on his person indicating injuries? For instance, was there any blood? Were there any bruises or abrasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not able to observe. As far as I can remember now, I could not observe anything more at that time, but he just told me that he had been beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When he stated that Mr. Landzo had beaten him, can you -- did he use the exact phrase "Mr. Landzo"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. "I was beaten by Zenga", he said, and he kept saying: "I'm choking. I'm choking."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Approximately when did this happen, if you know, that Mr. Samoukovic died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, I'm linking this to an important date, an important event that happened there, July 12th. So it was maybe four, five to six days possibly after the 12th. So maybe 15th July or 16th, 17th, 18th. I can't tell exactly. Anyway it was in the second half of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Had you seen Mr. Samoukovic at the camp at any time prior to the time that he was brought to the infirmary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think a few days before that I was going to Building Number 6 and I don't know who I was supposed to examine, but he didn't complain of anything. His appearance was quite decent, quite okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What happened to Mr. Samoukovic's body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what happened with his body. I can't remember now how much time he was left in the infirmary, nor where he was taken, nor how he was buried. I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you asked to fill out a death certificate for Mr. Samoukovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm really doing my best to give you an accurate account of what happened. The rule was under normal conditions for a death certificate to be filled out and a certificate for the burial, but what kind of death certificate could I write? What kind of injuries could I describe? What kind of a permit could I give? I beg you not to ask me these things, because I was not in a position to write anything, nor did I dare to write anything. That would mean writing out my own death warrant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, did anyone ever ask you -- anyone from the camp, not another prisoner, or anyone from outside the camp but not another prisoner, what happened to Mr. Samoukovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think on one occasion his daughter came to Ostrozac and asked me. I didn't want to give her any details. I just said that he had died.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you know whether or not anyone associated with the camp ever did any kind of investigation or questioned you or asked you any questions as part of any kind of investigation into what happened to Mr. Samoukovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: With respect to Mr. Avramovic or Mr. Mrkajic, were you aware of whether or not there was any kind of investigation into their deaths, or were you questioned about their deaths?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was asked about Cedo, what he had died of. I simply said, to expose myself to the least risk, as well as the other prisoners -- they kept asking who had killed him -- I said it was an infarction and things settled down immediately but later on an elderly man, somebody called Jovanovic -- I can't remember his name for a moment -- yes, Milovan, he was saying that he was climbing up this metal pole and he hit his head against the concrete floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned with respect to describing what happened to Mr. Samoukovic Mr. Landzo, named Zenga, and that he was a guard at the camp. Did you know Zenga's real name at the time that you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Mr. Landzo lived in the same street as me. I think he was living in the basement. I knew him as a boy who liked sports, and that is how I viewed him always. I never knew his name, nor did I know his surname, because I know that around the area of Glavaticevo there are three surnames to which he could belong: Lavic, Lulic and Landzo, three families in other words.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever learn what his real name was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was this after you left the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I fled from the territory of the municipality of Konjic on 16th October and later where I went there were no prisoners. So I really had no-one to talk to about this, but when I went to -- attended case courses in Belgrade, there were former inmates there, and then they started talking about these things, which, of course, was very painful to me, and it was then that I learned his real name.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm not going to ask you to give their names, but I just want to know whether or not while you were at the camp you were ever informed that other persons had died in the camp, even if you yourself did not treat the person or see the corpse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you rather than for you to tell everything that you heard from others, I'm just going to ask you specifically about a Mr. Petko Gligorevic. Can you tell us what, if anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. These questions require second-hand hearsay. The question itself says: "Have other people told you about things?" To answer these questions he will not be relying on his personal knowledge at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is correct, but, as I understand the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, hearsay may be permitted where it is reliable. I will bring out the facts such that this Chamber will be able to determine whether or not what is referred to in some systems as hearsay is reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the foundation has to be laid before we get into whether or not it is reliable. You can't get into it before you decide whether or not the foundation is reliable.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I may just briefly respond, I believe it is entirely appropriate and, in fact, the most efficient way and sometimes the only way to get out the information. The circumstances under which a person learns something will usually show the circumstances, and that it is almost impossible with respect to -- or if it's possible, it's unnecessary to try to in some sort of artificial or technical way bring out all the circumstances, because in general that will then also relate it. I think your Honours can hear the circumstances, including what was said, and determine if it's reliable, and then if you find it's not reliable, you can, of course, disregard it, but I think this continued objection to information and saying: "You must do A, B and C" is not necessary and it's not helpful for these proceedings. I think it's up to your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are laying down a very general rule. If he says: "I heard about some sort of particular person, about the death of that man", I can understand that that person can be examined. Merely saying "I heard other persons died"; that can be called not reliable or not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I agree with your Honour. I believe that in asking the questions the circumstances in which the witness learned this and from whom will be brought out. If not, I'll then ask any follow-up questions. So I'm not suggesting that your Honours should not hear the circumstances, including from whom. I'm just suggesting that the objections to the exact way it is done are not appropriate or necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that the Tadic Decision is pretty clear on that, and says that once there's an objection, the proponent of the evidence has to show reliability. Until there's an objection, anything comes in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It has to pass the test of reliability. Reliability has to be the source from where he receives the information so we can find out. Reliability is related to the source.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with your Honour and I agree with what Mr. Moran says but there's nothing in the Tadic Decision which says there is some sort of technical or exact way by which it is done, and I believe that normally when a witness describes something, the circumstances under which he received the information will come out, and that that is the most efficient way and the appropriate way to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us -- can you tell us from whom you learned something about Petko Gligorevic and the circumstances under which you learned it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned from the inmates that Petko Gligorevic on 27th, I think, in the morning died in prison, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. Your Honour, who -- the question "who" is not answered by saying "from the inmates". The foundation requirement is the reliability of the source. I don't think that source can just be "inmates", but has to be someone who can be identified. I therefore object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually some of our problems here is you wouldn't even allow the whole thing to be disclosed. When he might have finished, we would know exactly where he's going to. If it's not admissible, we will rule it out and it will not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I would ask counsel not to interrupt the witness during his answer. Sir, would you please continue with your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to rise to that. I'm entitled to object any time I want to, whether it is in the middle of a witness' answer or not, whether or not it is responsive to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Will you continue with your answer? . Thank you. Let's have your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: However, while I was under house arrest a member of the HVO came. He was known as Garo. I think his surname was Blazevic. I don't know his first name. He said: "Will you come with me to visit my parents?", who were in Donje Selo. I found Koviljka Mrkajic, and I saw that she was wearing black, and I asked what had happened, though I had learned that her husband had died in prison, Scepo Mrkajic. Then she said: "Yes, both my husband and my brother, Petko."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you have any relatives who are also related in any way to Mr. Petko Gligorevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Koviljka Mrkajic is my uncle (sic) and she's Petko Gligorevic's sister, and she told me she had attended his funeral.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, on another subject, let me ask you whether or not there was a detainee at the camp named Mr. Slavko Susic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was. Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what, if anything, you observed concerning the treatment of Mr. Slavko Susic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Slavko Susic twice, once from Building 22. On those beds we had slightly raised heads, so we could see through the window. I was looking through and I saw Mr. Delic and Mr. Landzo beating Susic, Slavko Susic. The second time I saw him was when I was asked to examine Sreten Zelenovic. I examined him and told him he had to take penicillin. He was taken out of building Number 9. He lay down on the concrete. I gave him a penicillin shot. I noticed that Slavko Susic was perhaps the third from the entrance. He was sitting on the left-hand side. I think he had beige trousers and mining boots rolled down, and his appearance was very bad. He was in very bad shape.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Which of these two occasions happened first? Did you first see Mr. Delic and Landzo beating Mr. Susic and then see him in Tunnel Number 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time I saw him when he was being beaten, and the second occasion was maybe a day later, when I was giving the shot, the penicillin shot.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go back then to the first occasion you saw Mr. Susic. When you say that you saw Mr. Delic and Mr. Landzo beating him, can you tell us more specifically what exactly you saw? For instance, did anyone have any sort of instrument with them? Can you just please tell us what you saw and what you heard yourself at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard a moan, but I didn't dare appear on the window, because if anybody were to see me, that would be the end of me. It was just a glance that I managed to catch.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: During your glance were you able to observe if anybody -- if there was any -- if either of Mr. Delic or Mr. Landzo had any kind of instrument?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Delic had.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Had you please just tell us what exactly you saw Mr. Delic had and what, if anything, he was doing with the instrument?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him waving this blunt object. What it was I can't tell. Actually I don't recollect.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you say "waving it", was he waving it far away from Mr. Susic or close to Mr. Susic? Can you just give it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Can you ask him whether he does --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Not translated).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He ended his last sentence by "he did not recollect". Is it the whole incident or what he was waving?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, when you say you "don't recollect", is it you don't recollect what happened or you don't recollect exactly what this blunt instrument was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't exactly remember what kind of blunt object it was, because they had baseball bats and they had -- we called them electric poles. Then there were the legs of chairs, the backs of chairs and tables, planks, shovel handles and all kinds of things. So I can't recollect exactly. Those were the objects that were used for beating.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not sure whether -- you started to answer this and it wasn't translated or what. Are you able to say anything about what you mean when you say you saw Mr. Delic waving this blunt instrument? For instance, how close he was to Mr. Susic. Did it appear that he was waving it towards Mr. Susic or just waving it in the air? Can you just tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: When somebody has already told you he merely had a glance, I don't know what you want him to say here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me be more specific. Sir, how far away, if you can say, was Mr. Delic in relation to Mr. Susic when you saw him waving this blunt instrument?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Close to him, close.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Then you stated you saw Mr. Susic later and that he was in a bad condition. Can you, if you can, tell us anything more specifically about what you observed such that you say he was in a bad condition?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think let us end here for lunch. We will come back to obtain the long statement after lunch.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. You can continue with your ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Sir, immediately before the lunch break you were -- we were discussing Mr. Slavko Susic. Could you please explain what you -- when you say you saw him in Tunnel 9 and he was in bad condition, what you were able to see with respect to his condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had an aspect of exhaustion and just of very bad condition, somebody -- a prisoner who was very drained and exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you able to see any sort of marks or abrasions or contusions on his body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. I could not see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Did you subsequently learn from anyone working in the camp anything about what happened to Mr. Susic?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. That question requires a hearsay answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I continue, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Did you hear anything --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the objection is he has no personal knowledge. He has already testified what he saw happened to Slavko Susic. What she is asking now is what he heard from no one particular person, just in general, which is what we covered earlier on our objection. So he's not going to be testifying through personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, under the Tadic Decision, I think she has to prove the reliability of the second-hand testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe his answers will describe the circumstances under which -- about how he learned what he heard, and your Honours can decide whether or not you believe that's reliable. The prosecution believes the circumstances will indicate that it is reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The way you put the question, I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: In fact, thus far all I've asked him is if he learned anything. I haven't even yet asked him what, if anything, he learned. So certainly to the extent I was obligated to do it in some sort of specific way, the question before the witness right now is: did he ever learn anything from anyone working in the camp about what happened to Mr. Susic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you can put such a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there needs to be some resolution with regard to this issue. I will remind the court that before lunch when a similar kind of question was asked, Ms McHenry informed the court that she would be able to show that it came from a reliable source. That source turned out to be the wife of a cousin of the person that we were talking about, who was never at Celebici, and who knows where she might have heard it from and who she might have heard it from? So I think the only way that this court is going to be able to judge the reliability of the source is for the prosecution to first identify the source and whether it is direct knowledge or whether it's gone through half a dozen people before it got to this witness. I think it is totally improper, as the Prosecutor suggests, that we first elicit the evidence and then try to convince you that it's reliable. I think the cart is before the horse. I think the horse has to come first, that is the foundation that it is reliable. Then the evidence can come in if you are satisfied with reliability. That seems to me to be the logical way to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think for me or the Trial Chamber to rule before hearing what the witness is saying is also putting the cart before the horse. We should know what is being suggested before we talk about the reliability, because it's not enough merely to say that he cannot say any particular thing because you think he cannot say such things. When he volunteers whatever the question is, we will be able to know. If it is not acceptable, we will say it should not be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But why don't you first ask: did anyone talk to him about the condition of Susic?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, I'm happy ... Sir, soon after you saw Mr. Susic, did you overhear guards at the camp discussing what happened to Mr. Susic? Sir, if you could just now indicate whether or not you did overhear guards discussing what happened to Mr. Susic soon after you saw Mr. Susic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first found out that Susic died and I found that out from Zarko Mrkajic, who is a detainee, because we together went to collect food. Sometimes I would go to get the food; sometimes he would go. When we would meet to take over the food, then I heard that he had died. Only later did I hear the guards laughing and one of them said: "Macic finished him off because of the goats". That's all I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you tell us with respect to your overhearing the guards, approximately, if you know, how long after you had seen Mr. Susic in the tunnel was -- did you hear this conversation between the guards?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a moment --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most probably within two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has to say the entire conversations which he overheard, because he might have heard just a passing sentence, which will not be explainable, the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Not even the connecting bit, what has happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, can you recollect -- can you tell the Chamber exactly everything that you recollect about what you overheard the guards saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already said that. I said what I heard and who I got information from that Slavko had died.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Now how -- did that person from whom you had the information see him die? Did they see him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You see, once you get into this hearsay, then you have to do other things then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zarko Mrkajic was also a detainee in Number 9 where Slavko Susic was staying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is possible he has also heard it the way you have heard it from him. We need somebody who actually was involved and knew that he had died and saw it, because, you know, hearsay upon hearsay upon hearsay will lead us nowhere. We want to have somebody whose evidence must be reliable, to hear from him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zarko Mrkajic was also in Number 9, where Slavko was, so he was there, and he passed on this information to me. That was the person who was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Sir, going on, you have -- you previously described seeing Mr. Delic with a blunt instrument standing close to Mr. Susic. Was there any other occasion when you saw Mr. Delic with any kind of instrument?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Delic some time -- I think it was August 3rd, 1992. On that occasion Risto Zuza was brought. He was a mental patient, a very difficult case. Then he had something in his hand, and he had a stick in his hand, something that we called the electric stick.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am going to try to go a little slowly. You stated that Risto Zuza was a mental patient, a difficult case. Was Risto Zuza also a detainee at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was, only he was at Musala, in the Sports Hall in Musala, Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Zuza at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He came that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me also just clarify before we go forward, sir. When you say he had something you called the electrical stick, who was it who had this electrical stick in their hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Delic. I can describe that. It's about two packs of cigarettes big and there was a button somewhere, and he would approach Risto, and when he would push this button, there would be some clonic spasms, and Risto would sort of be thrown into the corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: How many times did you see Mr. Delic use this instrument on Mr. Zuza approximately, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to this entire line of questioning. I can't find this man's name anywhere in the indictment. I don't think it's relevant to anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, his name is not specifically in the indictment, but it is a specific count in the indictment: inhumane acts involving the use of an electrical device. Mr. Delic is charged with using this device on many detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that they list two in these counts by name, 42 and 43, and -- I could be wrong, and I do stand to be corrected, but this, I think, is the first I've heard about, one, this person, and two, I think -- and again I stand to be corrected -- I think this is the first I've heard about this electrical device. If you're going to have evidence of other bad acts, maybe you ought to have some evidence first of bad acts that are alleged in the indictment. I understand that the Rules of Evidence of the Tribunal allow evidence of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't know whether we can exhaust inhumane acts?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Pardon me, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I am saying I don't know whether we can exhaust acts that are inhumane. It's infinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Because we never know what devices could come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Counts 42 and 43 specifically allege inhuman acts involving an electrical device.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is a specific one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It is a specific allegation involving two specific people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Your objection is that the name now did not appear in that indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: My objection is there is no legal or logical relevance on Mr. Zuza. Surely there is no legal or logical relevance until the Prosecutor introduces some proof that the acts charged in the indictment were committed. Like I say, I understand that the Rules of the Tribunal allow for evidence of a pattern of serious violations to bolster the prosecution's case but first I think the prosecution has to have a case to bolster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I see your argument is that the name there is not a name in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: This is all, that the act is inhuman. It is not what you are arguing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, what my argument is: is while it may be possible and the Trial Chamber may in its discretion admit evidence of patterns to bolster the Prosecutor's case, I don't think we start bolstering the Prosecutor's case until such time as the Prosecutor has introduced some evidence to prove the count in the indictment that we are trying to bolster. It would be -- until such time as the Prosecutor presents some evidence that Milenko Kuljanin and Mr. Dordic were -- had this machine used on them, I don't think that there is anything relevant to evidence that it occurred at some other occasion. The only reason that the Rules of Evidence allow evidence of pattern is to show that -- to help prove the allegations in the indictment, to help the Prosecutor or allow the Prosecutor to do that. Until we've had some proof of the allegations in the indictment, this extraneous acts evidence is just not relevant to anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I'm not so sure, but my reading of that count is that it was not limited to just those two persons mentioned in there. It was not limited to the two persons mentioned in there. It's broader than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: "Many detainees".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: "Many detainees".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, recalling that I did not join the defence team until some time right before the trial, I would suggest that this doesn't give him the written notice that the Statute and the Rules require if you say "and it could happen to anybody".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose there are very many and if you keep on indicating each of them, perhaps the whole indictment might be filled with those who have been treated that way. What was done was just to give specific names, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I understand that. I would just suggest that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You would have objected to that type of formulation of the count.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, I would suggest, if they can just prove what happened to any old person in there to prove that count, that we're not getting the kind of notice of the charges that the Statute and the Rules require that we be given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. None other than those names there should be added.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think when the Prosecutor, what, a year and a half ago formulated this indictment, they should have said who they said that these people injured, who the victims were. This is not Auschwitz. There is a limited number of people here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: If it had been challenged on the basis of vagueness, then one would have understood, but I think it's not vague now. At least there are two specific persons indicated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I have no problem, your Honour, with the two specific persons indicated there, the two named persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The point of your argument is that no other person should be added other than the two specific persons indicated in the count.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, if we are going to have the notice of -- the Statute and Rules require that we be given the notice of what we have to defend against.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The charge against you was he was in possession of an electrical device and he was using it against the detainees. That is the gravamen of the charge and that is what she is trying to prove by this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The gravamen of the charge is he used it against these two people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Other detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: We have been given notice of two people; put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may just say one thing: certainly it is very clear it is on many detainees, and that's what the defence has notice of. It is also the case, and had the defendant wished to challenge this, the indictment, it would have had to be with preliminary motion, and, in fact, there were preliminary motions filed by the Delic defence challenging the indictment and they were rejected. So whatever argument was made or should have been made, I think the indictment is very clear as "many detainees", and I think the witness should be allowed to continue his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let him continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I believe you were -- if my memory serves me correctly, you were describing this device?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please continue with your description and what you observed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, this is a device, size about two packs of cigarettes, with a button on the side. Later I was told by some people that this was used for -- when the cattle was slaughtered, and I saw that this was causing the tonic and clonic spasms and Risto fell into the far corner of this room.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You indicated that you believe this happened approximately around August 3rd. Can you tell us how it is that you are able to remember that approximate date and what the ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 2nd August -- that is the celebration of my father's Christian name and so I remember this date -- my father was still in prison and my brother was still in prison. My relatives were still imprisoned, but I think it was on 3rd August that Mr. Mucic's birthday was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was Mr. Mucic present on August 3rd in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was his birthday and he was there on his birthday. He even talked to me. He have even invited me to sit down at the table. He offered me a drink and something to eat. There was roast lamb that was being offered then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not anyone was filming any part of the birthday celebration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mucic had a camera and part of it was filmed, of this celebration.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was Mr. Mucic present when Mr. Delic was using this electrical device against Risto Zuza?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Was -- what else, if anything, did you observe on this day concerning what happened to Mr. Zuza?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then later Risto was forced to sing some folk songs and after that there was nothing in particular with Risto.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you present during the entire birthday celebration, or did you leave at the end of your -- at the end of the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left at the end of the day. They drove me off.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, was there -- at Celebici was there a detainee named Zeljko Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was. There was Zeljko Milosevic. He was in Building Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Chamber what, if anything, you yourself observed about the treatment of Zeljko Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw in the same way through the window of Building Number 22. I climbed and I saw Delic and Mr. Landzo kicking -- I saw them kicking Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was anyone else present at the time they were with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please describe just in more detail exactly what you saw happen, for instance where it was, if there was anything besides feet being used, how long it lasted? Will you please just give us everything you remember about this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I keep repeating that I did not dare stay at this window. Sometimes we would see prisoners from Number 9 when they would bring them out to wash up, and then later when we would hear moans, we would look up. We did not dare stay there, because if somebody would see us at the window, somebody of the guards, we knew what would follow. So this is what I saw. I saw him being kicked.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please tell us where it was that he was being kicked, I mean in other words what part of the camp now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Behind Number 9, Building Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Again without getting into what exactly was told to you, did anything ever happen to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Later we learned, because detainees from Number 9 would come for examination to us in Building Number 22, and when they would sit down to be examined, some of the injured would always ask: "What is happening up there in Building Number 9?", and then they would respond. They responded: "Milosevic died."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you remember any specific person who reported that Mr. Milosevic had died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Dragan Mrkajic. He was a detainee in Building Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mrkajic see the body of Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't discuss that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: How soon after you saw the beating of Mr. -- the beating of Mr. Milosevic did Dragan Mrkajic report that Mr. Milosevic had died, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now previously, sir, you mentioned Mr. Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Delic very well, and especially his father, his mother, because I often came to treat his mother and father at home. They were decent people. He would come to see me to ask for sick leave, because he was helping his father, who had retired rather early. They had a carpenter's shop and in order to earn some money he would ask for sick leave. I always satisfied his request.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What was Mr. Delic's role at the camp, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know he was deputy commander of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know. All the guards would always address him for anything. He would take from us lists of medicines. He would bring us whatever he did bring in. Then he would bring in a detainee to Building Number 22. I know that he brought by car Branko Gotovac, an old man who had been beaten up. He had an enormous hernia, incarcerated hernia on the right-hand side, and I know he drove him over. Then he brought another elderly man, Milorad Jovanovic also by car.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, when you first came to the Celebici camp in June, did you notice anything about Mr. Delic's physical condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Delic was limping on one foot. I don't exactly remember which one, but he was limping anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About twice --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About twice he called me into his office, because he was having pain in that leg, and I told him which of the analgesics he should use, and he would lie down.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, was there a detainee named Mr. Simo Jovanovic at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was. He's an elderly man. He was in Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to ever see Mr. Jovanovic and his physical condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was -- I did have the occasion to see Mr. Jovanovic. He was in poor condition. He had been beaten up. He had some broken ribs. His general condition was very poor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you estimate approximately when this was that you saw Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure of the dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know if it was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know if it was when you were a prisoner or when you were under house arrest going to the camp for work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was a prisoner. It happened while I was a prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you able to treat Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I examined him, all I had on me was some painkillers, and I informed Mr. Delic that he should be transferred to Building Number 22.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What happened after you requested that Mr. Jovanovic be transferred to Building 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After a few days Mr. Jovanovic died.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was he ever -- before he died, was he transferred to Building 22, as you had requested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was not transferred.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to remember at this time every prisoner and every injury you treated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A good share of those prisoners, some of those names I don't remember because I saw them for the first time in prison. Some of them I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: With respect to the ones you do remember, sir, do you remember whether or not you ever treated any prisoners who had suffered burns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did have occasion to see. They were Nedjelko Draganic, a boy of some 19 years of age, 18 or 19. He had burns on his lower legs and partly his upper legs. They were in -- blisters were infected. I treated them and he came for bandaging a couple of times. Then Spaso Miljevic came too. He showed me his burns on his lower legs, partly above the knee too. He had blue jeans rolled up -- no, not jeans -- a track suit that was rolled up about his knees. Then Momir Kuljanin who also had burns, and he was lying in Building Number 22. He had burns on his palms, on the palms of his hands. Momir came in the infirmary twice, on two occasions. Then he had an ulcer in his stomach, an ulcer that was bleeding. Then also Mirko Dordic came for burns. You could see his lips were burned, his tongue, and pincers had been placed in his ear, heated pincers and there was pus coming out of the ear.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, were there any women in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were women in the camp. Let me see. There was Grozda Cecez, Milojka Antic....

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not going to ask you for the names of all the women. Let me just ask you again without saying what you heard, can you please tell us whether or not you received any information at the camp suggesting that any of the women at the camp had been sexually assaulted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me go forward. From whom did you receive this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion I was in the office and a secretary was working there. That was after my release. I was under house arrest. That was when I learned about this. In the command building the secretary was Ismeta Posder and she told me that Mr. Delic was keeping Milojka Antic for himself and that Milojka Antic was a virgo intacta. That is a medical term. The traditional term is a virgin.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Mr. Delic have any conversation with anyone about the women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I heard. I was present in the room. This was also from the period from I was under house arrest, and when I came on certain days. It wasn't every day that I came to Celebici. Standing in the room, together with somebody -- I think he was called Nurko -- I can describe the man, what he looked like -- and there were another one or two people in uniform there, and they were talking in disguised terms of a lady whom they had taken to the hairdresser's, where she had a shower, and later, on the basis of their conversation, I deduced that it must have been Grozda Cecez.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please tell us exactly what you can remember about this conversation, in other words who said what as best you can recollect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "How did you like the lady?" In that sense was the question put to Mr. Nurko. Nurko was working -- was a person looking after the weapons, and I saw him for the first time in the command building.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who was it who said: "How did you like the lady?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was anything else said about how it was that the guard Nurko was able to be with this lady? Was anything said about that and, if so, please tell us exactly what was said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't recall any other details, nor did I really overhear the rest of the conversation, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was there anything said about whether or not Mr. Delic had any contact with this particular woman that was being talked about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, were you -- while you were at the camp, were you permitted to treat whoever you believe needed treatment, or did you have to ask permission to treat certain detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not able to extend treatment. Sometimes I was taken there to see a particular person in Building Number 6. Once I know I went to Number 9, and later the guards of the camp would select individual injured prisoners and bring them for treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Besides Simo Jovanovic, whom you have already testified about, was there any other occasion where you were not permitted to treat or transfer a detainee that you specifically requested be treated or transferred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Once I was taken to examine Milovan Kuljanin, Mici. I may be wrong with the first name. He was lying there beaten up and he had defecated in his -- fully dressed. He had urinated too. I asked Mr. Delic to have him transferred to Building Number 22. After some time -- it may have been an hour or an hour and a half -- Pavo Mucic came and asked: "Why didn't you transfer Mici to Number 22?" I said I had asked Mr. Delic to do it. Then I can't remember whether he was brought over by car or whether he was carried to Building Number 22. He spent quite some time in Building Number 22.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you remember when this incident was, what month or whether or not this was during the time you were a prisoner or under house arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the camp at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: As a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a prisoner, yes. As a prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Besides what you have already testified to, do you have any -- excuse me. What was Mr. Mucic's role in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We all called Mr. Mucic "Commander". I don't know anything more about his function, but I know that we all called him "Commander"; both the guards and we did. I did hear, that's true, on two occasions when I went to visit Mr. Delic in the command building saying that his leg hurt -- I saw the scar but no external signs of the trismus, that is the lower leg, and Music was sitting there helping to lift his leg and massage it, but we called him "Mr. Commander". This applies to Mr. Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is it the case -- was this true the entire time you were at the camp, or only a portion of the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was in the camp and later. It was roughly the same -- it was the same later too.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Both when you were a prisoner and when you were under house arrest; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: How frequently did you see Mr. Mucic at the camp? Let me first ask you about the time that you were a prisoner in the camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't meet often. We maybe saw each other once in seven days, twice, maybe twice in a week, sometimes three times.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And how about during the time that you were under house arrest? How frequently would you see Mr. Mucic at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then I saw him I think a little more often, because Mr. Mucic, after I was transferred to house arrest, he came once ; I think this must have been 1st or 2nd September. He invited me to his office and he told me that I should write a list of the elderly and weaker or sick people, but he warned me. He said: "Be careful as to what you put down as the diagnosis, because both you and me could suffer consequences." Don't put for a young man of 18 that he has chronic prostate infection. You put down an appropriate diagnosis." So that is what I did. I was with Mr. Mucic when it was his birthday. I think twice he was in the vehicle when his driver was taking me back to Ostrozac.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me go back. Is it the case that Mr. Mucic ever came to Building Number 22 while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mucic I remember well. I should like to tell you a rather funny story. We found it funny, both of us. I think it was on that occasion that he brought to Building Number 22 the mother of injured Miroslav Kuljanin who had been wounded during the shelling of the Sports Hall in Konjic, and with him was Zoran Cecez. They went out, Zoran and Miroslav's mother, and he asked whether I needed anything, and I didn't pay attention. When Miroslav Kuljanin was being admitted on the back part of the gluteal area there were large abscesses. They were shrapnel wounds, punctured wounds and I needed a scalpel. Then Mr. Mucic said: "How on earth am I going to get you a scalpel? What can you do?" I said: "I need to make an incision." Then he took out of his pocket a knife and gave it to me and said: "It's very sharp. Use it if you can." I said I didn't need it, that I would do it with some scissors. In fact, that is what I did, and we laughed, because Mr. Mucic said: "A Cetnik doctor can't function without a knife."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When Mr. Mucic came to the hangar, did you ever ask, you or any of the prisoners, how they had received their injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only if I was asked how I had got my injuries. This was two or three days after I had arrived at the elementary school the Third of March. Then some people in uniform appeared from Split. They were speaking with a Dalmatian dialect. They asked me: "And what's wrong with you?" So I said I had fallen from a car. Then they shouted at me: "Why don't you tell the truth?" I repeated that I had fallen from a car. These people in uniform, one of them was tall, dark, and he had the letter "U" on the upper part of his camouflage uniform, and he said that the military police of the HVO would protect us. However, after they left, we heard that the HVO policemen were talking amongst themselves and saying that nothing should happen to us because they wanted to change -- exchange us for their own people who had allegedly been captured at Kupres.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me go back to the Celebici camp. Was there ever a period when there was no food for a sustained amount of time at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that was from 12th July 1992. At that time I don't know exactly whether it was seven or nine military policemen from the territorial defence who had been killed, military policemen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then we didn't receive food. Some people said that they got food but I know that we didn't get it for four or five days, not even a piece of bread. We had water, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you know whether or not anyone at the camp made efforts at some point to get food for the camp and, if so, would you please describe that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I remember well. This was in the morning, somewhere around 10.00, 10.30. There was a red telephone outside the window and Mr. Mucic was speaking loudly. I was sitting opposite that, and I heard him calling Major Kevric -- Sefik Kevric, asking him to deliver food. However, I know I heard him say: "I don't care what the command is saying. I want food to be brought to the people. It would be honest either to kill these people or to feed them."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic indicate that he had any fear for himself if food was not obtained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He said: "I'll not be held responsible for this."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was food obtained after this period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think in a day or two food arrived, and I know that they called me and I and my colleague went out, and there were loaves of bread, and a loaf was given for each detainee, and about 100 grams of liver-paste. I carried the loaves of bread, my colleague the liver-paste. However, when I entered, I told the detainees: "Be careful. We won't eat it all. We will share it among three detainees, one liver-paste among three and one loaf of bread among two." Then Mr. Delic appeared behind my back and said: "No, you have to eat up everything." Of course we did. We ate up the whole loaf and the whole liver-paste. Of course then we were thirsty. We were constantly knocking on the door. Mr. Macic, he did indeed let us go out and bring as much water as we needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am going to go to a new area. I don't know if you would like to take your break now or if you want to continue and take your break later. I just wanted to advise you of that fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: If it is convenient --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We should have our break at 4 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, your Honour. My memory is wrong. We can go to 4.00. I just didn't want to ask more questions and then have the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, you have indicated previously that on 22nd July you were permitted to leave the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I am going to ask you to describe exactly what happened when you were released, and I'm going to ask that you go slowly, and so if something is not clear about who you are talking to, I can ask. Please tell us what happened such that you were released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 22nd July some time around 10 o'clock -- around 11 o'clock a guard Fodil -- I don't know his last name; we called him Focak -- entered into Number 22. He had a piece of paper in his hands and he said to my colleague and myself: "Please collect your things. You will pay me a round for this, because you're going home." However, I would like to say that we had some indications that we could be released on that day. At first I did not believe my colleague, but he said that Mr. Delalic would send a car for us at 10 o'clock. This happened at 11 o'clock, and we --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Let me just be clear. When this person Focak said: "You are going to pay me a round for this", was he indicating that you were going to buy him a drink because you were being released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he said it jokingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As if we owed him a drink because of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I just wanted to clarify. Now when you say your colleague, do you mean the other doctor who was working in the infirmary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was it that same morning that he told you that he believed Mr. Delalic would be sending a car for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Please continue, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We left the building. It was a white jeep-type of vehicle. We went to the house belonging to Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you say "we", do you mean you and the other doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's what I have in mind. We entered into the room where Mr. Zejnil Delalic was, Mr. Dzemal Delalic, his brother, and in the other part of the room somebody was sleeping. Actually they were snoring. Later I was told by my colleague that this was the older brother of Zejnil. Mr. Zejnil offered us dinner. We told him we had eaten. He offered us drinks and I accepted a coffee, and my colleague sort of nudged me and he said: "Well, it will take a long time for it to be made and drunk, so why don't you take something alcoholic?" I said: "Okay. I will take a cognac." Mr. Delalic was wearing a camouflage uniform. He had just come back from Glavaticevo from the front. Mr. Zejnil Delalic then told the two of us to report to Mr. Ahmed Jusufbegovic for work. However, I think the next day I did not report to Dr. Ahmed Jusufbegovic, and the day I did report to him -- I think it was a Sunday -- I called on the phone. I used the phone of a Muslim person, because the Serb -- the phones of the Serbs in Konjic were disconnected at that time. I asked whether Mr. Jusufbegovic was at work. He said that -- I was told that he was. Then I went to the Health Centre and I found him there in front of the dentistry. Outside there was Dr. Jusufbegovic Sead Hajduk, who was a dentist, and Dr. Rif Sarajlic. He called me off and he told me to follow him to his office, which at that time was on the premises of Hygienic Service. We were followed by Dr. Hajduk, and Dr. Jusufbegovic told me at that time there is no way that I could start working again because colleagues do not want to have anything to do with me, not even to have to look at me. Then he offered to have me go back to the Celebici camp, and I started crying, and I said: "Don't even mention this." I said I would stay in Konjic. So at that I left and went back to my apartment, which had already been occupied also by a colleague, who was a Muslim, and several days later I asked Fadil Spago, the Commander of the police station, whether I could move to the village of Ostrozac in Jablanica Municipality, and he allowed me. He gave me permission to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me go back for a moment. When you stated that you were at Celebici on July 22nd and the guard Focak came in with a paper, were you given that paper and, if so, what was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did receive a piece of paper, where it was written that I was not a member of the SDS, that is I guess the political party. I don't want to be reminded of this paper. That I was not a member of a terrorist organisation, and I showed this paper to Mr. Delalic at his apartment. He took this paper and he wrote on it. He added: "He continues to care for the injured prisoners." Then he asked me where I would be and I asked him not to write in the direction in which I would be moving, because Mr. Delalic knew where my wife was from, and he -- and I asked him not to do that so I could go and visit her occasionally. He agreed to that, and then I had this piece of paper when I escaped.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now whose signature -- whose name appears on this piece of paper as authorising your release?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On this piece of paper it is written "Zejnil Delalic" and Mr. Delalic accommodated me at that time and he -- I also know that once when the television of Bosnia came, they filmed a conversation with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me stop for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. You are talking about the contents of a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Where is that document?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That's my next question. May I ask the help of the Registrar? May I ask that this be marked for identification purposes? I have extra copies of the document and a translation. This document has previously been provided to all defence counsel. (Handed). So the record is clear, the witness is being shown a document marked for identification purposes as Prosecution Exhibit 154. Sir, I ask whether or not you recognise what that document is and, if so, if you'll please tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The release document on the basis of which I was released from the prison. In the lower left corner it says: "Continues to care for the injured prisoners". This is what Mr. Delalic wrote later on when we were in his apartment. Here it says "29th May", as if I had been captured -- that's "arrested" there, but it was 26th when I was actually arrested, but here it states 29th.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, is this the document you have been testifying about that you were given at the camp, and then Mr. Delalic later added to it in his apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would move into evidence Prosecution Exhibit 154?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can tender it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any further questions about this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: "Chief of Investigating Body"; who would that be?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Delalic is cited as chief of the investigating body.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I think it says hand-written "for Chief of the Investigating Body". I believe that some of the prior testimony indicates that this refers to this investigative commission, which was present in the first couple of weeks of the camp's existence. Sir, did you ever see Mr. Zejnil Delalic at the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Mr. Delalic about two or three weeks after I had been released into the house arrest.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please describe the circumstances under which you saw Mr. Zejnil Delalic at the camp, and again I will ask that you please go slowly so if I want to clarify who you are talking about or anything, I may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One morning when I was brought in a vehicle to the Celebici camp from the house where I was under house arrest I saw in front of the command building a guard, who told me to come into the command building, and my colleague and myself were in this room, and together with us there there was Mr. Zejnil Delalic, Mr. Sefik Delalic and I cannot recall -- yes, there was Jandranka Milosevic, and a man who introduced -- presented himself as Zvonko Maric. They were the journalists of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I just clarify, sir? Is it the case that Mrs. Milosevic and Mr. Maric were the journalists from the Bosnian television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Please continue, sir, with what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Zejnil Delalic offered us to sit down. Then he asked what we would like to drink, coffee, juice or something alcoholic. They had real home-made plum brandy. I think we only took coffee and I think I have may have taken juice as well. He asked about the conditions of prisoners and I said: "At this moment it's not so bad, given the previous condition." He said -- "given what their previous condition was". He said would I restate that in front of the camera. I did that and so did my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, did you feel that you were able to tell the truth, the entire truth about what was happening in Celebici when you were being interviewed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I felt very awkward. It was very difficult for me because I had to measure every word. Otherwise it was clear what would have happened to me, but to a degree I did say some things about the conditions. Well, you see these prisoners, as I already said, what conditions we were living in, what equipment we had and for them to recover, everybody would want a doctor who was teaching at the military medical school. Let me just tell you -- let me mention just some of the procedures that are recommended in the book about how to care for the victims of war, and it was -- which was issued by the Red Cross, which I received in February and March of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me just ask you: is it correct that -- rather than have you get into detail about the procedures -- is it correct that -- is it a fair summary that the procedures that were recommended were not carried out in the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please clarify that question a little bit for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, when you -- actually if you -- with you -- if I may, let me just go forward again, sir. Other than the occasions that you have testified to, did you ever have -- excuse me. Let me go forward. You indicated before, sir, that at some point you created a list pursuant to Mr. Mucic's request with the prisoners who were in the worst state of health; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I put together a list and this list was later taken by Mr. Mucic, and he took this list. On one occasion I was in his private vehicle with him when we stopped by Mr. Delalic's house and then he took that list upstairs to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was everybody on the list that Mr. Mucic took to Mr. Delalic's house put on the list by you because they were in bad physical condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There were people there whom I put down, but there were ten categories, as I already said, and persons in the first three categories could not be released. From the other categories they could be released, and some of those -- and I don't know what was the criteria and whether it was personal, the choice -- but they were put on the list by Mr. Mucic and he told me to put them down for some -- Mr. Delic also told me to put them down. This only worked for two or three days. Following that they were released without any examination or based on personal choice of Mr. Delic and Mr. Pavo Mucic or their own standards.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, while you were working in the camp, was there ever a time when conditions at the camp got noticeably better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, sometimes -- four or five days before my release you could sort of notice a difference, because the families were allowed to bring in food. However, I did see -- there was a metal door -- there was a metal door at Building Number 22 and there was a crack underneath about 5 cm. So we -- so the ones of us who felt a bit better would sort of lie down and look out, and so we called it a look-out. So the guards would take this food that was being brought to the gate. It was put into a car, a Fiat make, and I saw that -- I saw these plastic bags. A lot of them would just go straight into the garbage container, but I saw some of them, and again I don't know if there were some personal connections or personal -- some of the people would get these plastic bags with food.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry. Am I correct in understanding you that it was in the middle part of July that people were sometimes allowed to receive food from outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, four or five days before I was released I noticed that it started little by little, that it was permitted that the food could be brought in, but this food for one part would end up in containers, and what we would end up with would be dry bread. When I would smell it, you could see that there was a piece of roast meat there, but we would only get some bread, maybe an onion. No cigarettes could come through. Some pieces of clothing, no underwear. Later somehow it passed through.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So people would get something.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is it the case that Celebici was ever visited by the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Red Cross came I think on 12th August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can I ask you, sir, was there any change -- did you notice anything about conditions in the camp after the Red Cross came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was a huge difference. I know when I came the first time, when I first came to the camp, I greeted a tall gentleman. He had a beard, he had glasses on. I think he was Dutch. That was the first day and I was with him in building Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can I just clarify: when you -- is this the first time the Red Cross came to the camp or the first time that you came to the camp that you saw this gentleman with glasses? I'm just trying to clarify. I think there may have been a translation issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was the first time when the Red Cross came. I know that there was a woman there. She introduced herself as a nurse, a medical nurse. The next day I was given a letter through the Red Cross where people were enquiring about me from where I live now, people who lived there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were there any beatings in the camp after the Red Cross came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came the next morning, I saw that the prisoners were dejected, and I asked them what it was, and they told me that they were beaten and that they would not talk to the Red Cross representatives any more.
