I told them not to do that, because they would just be doing damage to themselves and this was an international organisation and they should co-operate. Then they agreed to that. Then later, that's the day after they departed from the Celebici camp, the conditions in the camp improved considerably. There was no beatings like before. Sporadically there were still some beatings, but not like before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that you worked at the camp until some time in October. Were you going to the camp daily at this time and why was it that you stopped working in the camp completely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first I would go almost every day, including Saturdays and Sundays. Mr. Zeljko Buric would come to get me, who was the personal driver of Mr. Pavo Mucic, and later maybe he was coming every other day, and later even less frequently, so that maybe I would go there once every seven days.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you stop working at Celebici completely when you escaped from the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think about four to seven days I was not going to Celebici, and that was an excellent opportunity for me to flee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mrs. McHenry, I think we will stop here and come back at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms McHenry, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours, and I am almost finished. Sir, after you left the Konjic area and escaped in October 1992, have you ever had any contact with Mr. Mucic again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: On how many occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once he called. I was not at home. My daughter answered. Once he also called my wife's family and he called a third time and I answered the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When was it approximately that Mr. Mucic called you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the signing of the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What was the subject matter of the conversation, and in particular let me ask you whether or not Mr. Mucic indicated during the conversation that he was being investigated for war crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that he had been charged by the Muslims for some murders and that he had been proclaimed a Cetnik supporter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did he indicate anything about whether or not there were any current investigations into his activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you really need this evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that his relationship with Mr. Mucic, including the phone call and the letter, are very relevant, and I'm going to just briefly -- I'm just about finished with the phone call -- I'll be asking him about them. Sir, when Mr. Mucic called you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. Are you talking about the contact more than a year after he had left the Celebici camp. How would that be relevant in the context of what happened at Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe that it's relevant to show --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I can understand conduct immediately or soon after.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I can well understand if something happens immediately after he leaves the Celebici camp. How is it relevant, unless you want admissions from him?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe that the nature of the relationship between Mr. Mucic and this witness is relevant to evaluating the witness's credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But has he taken the position that Mucic is his friend?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, I don't believe that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How would that help us in determining the charges in relation to the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe, among other things, it could be evidence of the consciousness of guilt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is too long a jump.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I only have one other question, which will not have to do with the substance of what was said. Sir, during this conversation was anyone -- did you hear anyone else who was present with Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Present with Mr. Mucic was Petar Blazevic and his brother, Jerko.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Petar Blazevic, did he have any role in the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that Petar Blazevic before I came to Celebici had been a guard in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is hearsay evidence for which the foundation has not been properly laid by my learned friend. She must do so, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry. I don't believe it is hearsay evidence. I believe this witness heard Mr. Blazevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If you read what the answer was, it says: "I heard that..." I think that's hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That's fine, sir. Sir, going forward, when was the second time that you had contact from Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A month ago I received a letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. With the assistance of ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: This is, for the record, I believe Prosecution Exhibit 155. Sir, is that the letter you received from Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His signature is there and it was given to me by another person.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So am I correct, sir, it did not come to you through the mail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that this Prosecution Exhibit 155 be admitted into evidence, and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an objection to that letter being admitted as against my client, Mr. Landzo. If it is to be admitted at all, I would ask that the admission be restricted solely to an admission against Mr. Mucic. I'm not even sure it's admissible against Mr. Mucic, but certainly not against Mr. Landzo. It contains language in it about other defendants in this case that I think has no relevance, is inflammatory. I think perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. The prosecution has no objection and would only be seeking to introduce it against Mr. Mucic, if that helps any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I am not too sure even how it would be admissible against Mr. Mucic, because the witness claims that he received it through someone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That's right, your Honour. He received it through someone and I believe, though, that when you read the contents of the letter, as well as look at the signature, there is more than enough evidence for your Honours to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't see the signature. All I see here is "Pavo".

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe "Pavo" is all it says, but I believe when you read the contents of the letter, it is clear because of the nature of what is discussed that it was written by Mr. Mucic, and if your Honours have -- and that there is more than enough evidence for you to find that it is reliable, and prima facie case was introduced against Mr. Mucic. If there is any evidence and your Honours want more, I would ask that Mr. Mucic be asked to provide handwriting samples so they can be compared with the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: A good fiction writer, a good novelist can write the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honours are being invited to be handwriting experts as well as judges of the International Tribunal. That is an interesting proposition, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We have to do that many times. In order to see if a document has been written by a particular person is always a matter for the court to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes, but upon evidence. There has to be evidence before you can come to the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is it the case that this letter has not been written by your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I make no admissions whatever. I respectfully submit before you can make the leap between someone simply proffering it to you and saying it is a fact there has to be some evidence to prove it. There is not such evidence and the prosecution cannot, in my respectful submission, force Mr. Mucic to do anything such as providing handwriting samples. It's their case. They must prove it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: What about the person who gave it to the evidence, through who he has received it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy to ask. Did the person who delivered this identify themselves or did you -- do you know who it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, she did not introduce herself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe when you look at the contents of the letter that although you can say that fiction writers can write anything, the issue is: is there prima facie evidence that it is written by him, and I believe when you look at the specific information, they are things that are peculiarly within the knowledge of Mr. Mucic in their relationship, and I believe that is enough. If not, I would ask that your Honours direct Mr. Mucic to provide handwriting samples, because I find it inconceivable that a witness -- that an accused would be able to write such letters with material such as in here and then say: "And I refuse to give handwriting samples." I certainly believe, and we are happy to provide your Honours with legal authority, if you think it's necessary, that the accused be permitted -- be directed to provide handwriting samples, and if he refuses, that adverse inferences be drawn as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But, Ms McHenry, you are using it as an admission on the part of the accused, this letter?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Admission of what?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, among other things, that, for instance, Mr. Mucic was present at the time that the prisoners were moved from the Third of March School to Celebici. That would be, for instance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is that an admission of guilt or what? When you talk about admission, you talk about something which has --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It has some incriminating content. Is it incriminating in any way?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I believe certainly that is incriminating. It contains significant corroboration for what this witness has said. I also see that in there at another point the accused admits that he was commander at least as of 3rd August. I believe that also is an admission. I don't believe it's the case that an accused has to say: "I'm guilty; I did it", for it to be an admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Your argument is that if you make an allegation, it is for the accused person to refute it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: This is what you are suggesting. You should now prove to a handwriting expert that he did not write it when you have not even shown sufficiently that he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe on the face of this and the contents of this are such that it was written by Mr. Mucic because of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: What makes it clear? What makes it clear?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: For instance, his discussion about what happened on 3rd March; for instance, his discussion about what's happened in trial. I think, for instance, his discussion about what he did with respect to this witness. So I don't -- I believe that that is sufficient evidence, and if it's not, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You think this witness cannot write that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, I believe that's a matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: These are some of the things you have to have in mind when it's ambiguous. It can come from either side.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that this court can use its common sense and make reasonable inferences. To the extent that your Honours disagree, I believe that the prosecution is entitled to ask your Honours to give -- for the accused to give a handwriting exemplar, and for you to find otherwise is to give all the accused carte blanche to do what they wish, including writing threatening letters, that are of no evidence whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I hear you. The Trial Chamber -- I don't know if a prima facie -- I don't know. I find it difficult to accept this as sufficient evidence that it is written by him. I don't think so, because there's nothing which links him with it, other than the name "Pavo", because all the contents are contents which are not a monopoly of his. All the indications, all you have said are transactions he had with other people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: For instance, your Honour, I would also point out the fact that -- your Honour, I believe that there are many facts in there which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Which only he can know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That's right. If your Honours disagree, then I'm asking under -- excuse me. I'm sorry, your Honours. The Rules which indicate that your Honours can make orders to direct the accused to give a handwriting sample -- I'm sorry, your Honours, for my delay. I would be referring to Rule 54 and I would ask that your Honours direct the accused to provide a handwriting sample.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: This is monstrous, absolutely monstrous. Does your Honours -- do your Honours recall Article 21(4)(G), which requires this man not to be compelled to testify against himself or to confess guilt? Are your Honours seriously going to take the pretty general wording of Rule 54 and say that he can be forced to provide evidence against him? In my submission this is the most monstrous suggestion I have heard in this court to date. I invite your Honours to reject it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I can briefly respond, it is well settled law in many jurisdictions, including the United States, including the United States Supreme Court cases, that the provision of handwriting exemplars does not violate the ban against self-incrimination or the right not to incriminate yourself. If your Honours wish legal briefs on that, I'm happy to do that. I don't believe it's necessary. I believe it is well-established law in many jurisdictions that an accused can be directed to provide handwriting exemplars without violating the ban against self-incrimination, and if the accused refuses to do so, then adverse inferences can be drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: There is no such rule in the Rules of Evidence and Procedure or the Statute. Again I invite your Honours to reject that submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will rise and come back in the next fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has just casually looked at this matter, but we find it difficult to come to a decision at the moment. We think the decision to admit it or not -- this letter or not, should be deferred until actually argument is gone into as to its admissibility because, as we have all observed, the relevance in the letter which suggests pointing some accusing finger, but at this stage is still a wavering pointer, and until the wavering settles, it is not possible to accept that it is that of the accused. There is a substantive argument about not incriminating himself. On the side of the prosecution is the argument that there is prima facie evidence, but I suppose that is not enough for admissibility. So we will defer the admission until parties have actually submitted good written and oral arguments in support of the proposition.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Maybe just in connection with that, the letter refers to a newspaper article. Just so that the record is clear, I would ask that this be shown to defence counsel and then shown to the witness, and then I'll just admit this in case it later becomes relevant as part of this. Again we will not be seeking to admit it now. We will just be seeking to have it as an attachment to the extent it becomes relevant. I'll also advise your Honours that there is no translation of this article, but we will request that one be prepared by the translation section as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Again, your Honours, I assume there is no effort by the prosecution to have this document admitted against anyone but the defendant Mucic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: How could it when it's not an admission by anyone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have finished with your examination-in-chief, apart from this letter?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I will just show the witness this article and ask if this is the article attached with the letter and then the prosecution is finished with examination-in-chief. Sir, I'm just going to ask if you recognise what that is? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): We would first like to know how the Prosecutor gained possession of these newspapers. To be able to offer them for identification, the Prosecutor would need to explain how they gained possession of this article, as I know the language and it has not been translated, and this article mentions the names of other people, and I don't know on what grounds the Prosecutor is offering this newspaper to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I thought you said it was attached to the letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That's correct. I believe that's what the witness will testify to. The prosecution got this exact -- this exact thing was given to the witness along with the letter and, in fact, the letter refers to a newspaper article, and for the present purposes we are just having it identified to the extent that it sheds any light on this or later becomes relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The witness is not going to find it very difficult to give that evidence now that the Prosecutor has just told him what evidence he is going to give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is fairly difficult. You could have, at the time you were tendering the letter, included the newspaper excerpt.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, five minutes ago, when I offered it, I suppose I could have, but because I didn't think that -- because I believed what was relevant was the letter and that had -- which contained the admissions, rather than the newspaper article, that it was unnecessary. Now if there's going to be some discussion about a deferred admission, then, your Honours, I think at the minimum we should have on the record what the newspaper article is. I mean, I, in fact -- I haven't seen a translation of this, so at this time, to the extent that what's at issue is what did this witness receive and what was attached to it, it may become relevant later. Obviously if it turns out to have no evidentiary value whatsoever, your Honours can disregard it, but since the witness is here now and all that is being done is the witness is identifying whether or not this is the article referred to in the letter, I don't see that there can be any prejudice, and, your Honours, if it is later determined that this is of no assistance whatsoever and of no relevance whatsoever, then your Honours can disregard it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The document is not in, so the thing which came with it can still be attached to it. It's not in yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, your Honour, I do understand that. Sir, can you tell us if you recognise what else been given to you as -- marked as 156 -- do you recognise that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what it is and when you received it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the same time as the letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I notice that there is some highlighting and a little bit of writing on that. Can you just tell me whether when you received that article it had the highlighting and the writing on it, or is that something that you yourself did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was there when I received it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay, your Honour. We would be -- we will defer tendering this until the subsequent proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That concludes the prosecution's examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We have worked out the order. We will proceed in the following way: first, counsel for Mr. Delalic; second, counsel for Mr. Mucic; third, counsel for Mr. Delic; and, fourth, counsel for Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours. We have been working for quite some time today. I am ready for the cross-examination, but, as my cross-examination will take much longer than these fifteen minutes, I would be very grateful if the court would agree that we begin with the cross-examination tomorrow morning. I think the witness has been exposed to a fire of questions all day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your indulgence. I think we can break off here and start tomorrow morning. I think 10.30. We will start at 10.30. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: --ooOoo--
